assignments.name: Build a complete HTML document
assignments.description:
## Give your page its proper skeleton **What you are making:** a complete HTML document — the same skeleton every professional web page in the world starts from, with a name that appears on the browser tab. **Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are. 1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* > **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-doc-structure-yourname`. 1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**). 2. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-doc-structure-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-doc-structure-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project: - `index.html` — your web page - `style.css` — how it looks - `script.js` — what it does For this assignment you only touch **`index.html`**. --- ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** replace what is in `index.html` with a complete, properly shaped document. 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Click anywhere in that big area. 3. Press **Ctrl + A** *(Mac: Command + A)*. Everything in the file turns blue — it is now selected. 4. Press **Backspace** *(the key above Enter, sometimes marked ←)*. The file is now empty. This is meant to happen. 5. Type the whole thing below, exactly as it is written. The spaces at the start of the indented lines are there to make it readable — copy them if you can, but nothing breaks if they are off by one. ```html My Page

Hello

This page has a proper skeleton now.

``` **What each piece means:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `` | Tells the browser *this is a modern web page*. Always the first line. Note the exclamation mark, and no space after `` … `` | Wraps the entire page. Everything else lives inside these two. | | `lang="en"` | Says the page is written in English. | | `` … `` | Information **about** the page. Visitors never see what is in here. | | `` | Tells the browser which alphabet to use. It is a lonely tag — no closing partner. | | `My Page` | The name shown on the **browser tab** at the top of the window. | | `` … `` | Everything people actually **see**. From now on, your work goes in here. | Tags shut from the inside out. `` closes before `` opens, and `` comes last of all — like boxes packed inside boxes. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. > You may change `My Page` to any name, and change the heading and paragraph words. Every tag, and the line ``, must stay exactly as written. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. Look at the **tab along the top of the browser window**. It should read **My Page** — not `index.html`. That is your `` doing its work. In the page itself you see the heading and the paragraph from inside `<body>`. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. Tab still says `index.html`? The `<title>` line is missing, is outside `<head>`, or the file was not saved. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Add the full HTML skeleton" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The browser tab still says `index.html` | The `<title>` is missing or sits outside `<head>` | `<title>My Page` must be between `` and `` | | Your heading appears in the browser tab instead of on the page | It was typed inside `` | `<title>` holds the tab name only — your `<h1>` belongs between `<body>` and `</body>` | | Red cross on "has doctype" | The first line is mistyped | It reads `<!doctype html>` — exclamation mark straight after `<`, no space | | VS Code draws a wiggly red line under `</html>` | A closing tag is missing or out of order | Check the order at the bottom: `</body>` then `</html>` | | The word `charset` shows up on the page | The `<meta>` line lost one of its angle brackets | The whole line must sit between `<` and `>` | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] The very first line is `<!doctype html>` - [ ] There is an `<html lang="en">` and a matching `</html>` at the end - [ ] There is a `<head>` … `</head>` pair - [ ] `<title>` … `` sits inside the `` - [ ] There is a `` … `` pair with your heading inside it - [ ] The file is saved (no white dot on the VS Code tab) - [ ] The browser tab shows your title, not `index.html`

assignments.name: Build a form
assignments.description:
## Build a sign-up form people can type in

**What you are making:** a small sign-up form with a name box, an email box, a tick box and a button — the same set of parts behind every sign-up page you have ever filled in.

**Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.


---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-form-page-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-form-page-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-form-page-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you only touch **`index.html`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** put a working sign-up form on the page.

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right.
2. Find the line that says `<body>` and the line that says `</body>`. Everything you add goes **between those two lines**.
3. Click at the end of a line between them and press **Enter** to make a new line.
4. Type this:

```html
<form>
  <label>Name <input type="text"></label>
  <label>Email <input type="email"></label>
  <label>Subscribe to updates <input type="checkbox"></label>
  <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
</form>
```

**What each piece means:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `<form>` … `</form>` | Wraps the whole thing and marks it as one form. |
| `<input>` | A box the visitor types in. A lonely tag — there is **no** `</input>`. |
| `type="text"` | An ordinary typing box. |
| `type="email"` | A box that expects an email address. |
| `type="checkbox"` | A small square you can tick. |
| `<label>` … `</label>` | The words next to a box. Wrapping the box **inside** the label joins the two together, so clicking the words puts the cursor in the box. |
| `<button type="submit">` | The button that sends the form. The words between the tags are what is printed on it. |

Every box needs a label. A box with no label is a guessing game for the visitor, and unusable for anybody using a screen reader.

Clicking **Sign up** will appear to do nothing, or will blink the page. That is correct — there is nowhere yet to send the answers to.

**Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

> You may change the words *Name*, *Email*, *Subscribe to updates* and *Sign up*. Keep the `<form>`, the three `<input>` boxes, the `<label>` round each one, and the `<button>`.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page.
4. You should see the words *Name* with a typing box beside it, *Email* with another box, *Subscribe to updates* with a small empty square, and a button reading **Sign up**. Click inside the first box and type your name — the letters appear. Now click the **words** *Subscribe to updates*: the square should tick itself. That is the label doing its job.

Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload.

Boxes missing? Check each `<input>` sits between `<form>` and `</form>`, and that the file was saved.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add a sign-up form"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Clicking **Sign up** does nothing, or the page blinks | There is nowhere to send the answers yet | Nothing is wrong — sending forms comes much later |
| The boxes sit squashed side by side on one line | Labels and boxes are inline by nature | Normal at this stage. Spacing them out is a CSS job in a later course |
| Clicking the words does not tick the square | The `<input>` is outside its `<label>` | `</label>` must come **after** the box, so the box is inside the label |
| Red cross on "has a <button>" | You used `<input type="submit">` instead | Add `<button type="submit">Sign up</button>` inside the form |
| The email box complains when you press the button | `type="email"` expects an address with an `@` in it | Type something like `me@example.com`, or leave it empty |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] There is a `<form>` … `</form>` pair on the page
- [ ] There are three `<input>` boxes: text, email and checkbox
- [ ] Each `<input>` is wrapped in its own `<label>` … `</label>`
- [ ] There is a `<button type="submit">` … `</button>` inside the form
- [ ] Clicking a label's words puts the cursor in its box, or ticks its square
- [ ] The file is saved (no white dot on the VS Code tab)

assignments.description:
## Play a video inside your own page

**What you are making:** a page with a YouTube video playing inside it — a window cut into your page that shows another website through it.

**Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.


---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-media-page-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-media-page-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-media-page-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you only touch **`index.html`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** put a playable video on your page.

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right.
2. Find the line that says `<body>` and the line that says `</body>`. Everything you add goes **between those two lines**.
3. Click at the end of a line between them and press **Enter** to make a new line.
4. Type this as **one single line**. It is long — let it run off the edge of the screen and do not press **Enter** in the middle of it:

```html
<iframe width="560" height="315" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/aqz-KE-bpKQ" title="A video" allowfullscreen></iframe>
```

**What each piece means:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `<iframe>` … `</iframe>` | A window that shows **another web page inside yours**. Nothing goes between the two tags, but the closing tag is still required. |
| `width="560"` and `height="315"` | The size of that window, measured in screen dots called pixels. |
| `src="…"` | The address of the page to show inside the window. |
| `/embed/aqz-KE-bpKQ` | The part after `/embed/` is the video's own code. |
| `title="A video"` | A short description, read aloud to people using a screen reader. |
| `allowfullscreen` | Lets a viewer blow the video up to fill the screen. It stands alone — no `=` and no quotes after it. |

**To use a video of your own instead:**

1. Open YouTube in your browser and start any video.
2. Look at the address at the very top of the browser. It reads something like `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aqz-KE-bpKQ`.
3. The code is the part straight after `v=` — here, `aqz-KE-bpKQ`. If there is an `&` after it, stop at the `&`.
4. Replace `aqz-KE-bpKQ` in your `src` with that code, keeping `https://www.youtube.com/embed/` in front of it.

The address must say `/embed/`, not `/watch?v=`. A `/watch?v=` address gives you an empty grey rectangle.

**Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

> You may use any video code you like, and any numbers for `width` and `height`. The tag must stay an `<iframe>` with a `src` that starts `https://www.youtube.com/embed/`.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page.
4. You should see a black rectangle with a large play button in the middle. Click it — the video plays, inside your own page.

Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload.

An empty grey or white rectangle? The address uses `/watch?v=` instead of `/embed/`, or your computer is not connected to the internet — this one needs a connection.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Embed a YouTube video"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| An empty grey or white rectangle | The address uses `/watch?v=` instead of `/embed/` | The `src` must read `https://www.youtube.com/embed/CODE` |
| The words *Video unavailable* inside the rectangle | That video's owner does not allow embedding | Pick a different video and swap its code into the `src` |
| Nothing at all appears on the page | `</iframe>` is missing | The closing tag is required even though nothing sits between the tags |
| The video is tiny, or far too big | `width` and `height` are measured in pixels | Change 560 and 315 to other numbers and reload |
| Red cross on "has an <iframe>" | The line was broken in two by pressing **Enter** | It must be one unbroken line starting `<iframe ` |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] There is an `<iframe` … `</iframe>` on the page
- [ ] Its `src` starts with `https://www.youtube.com/embed/`
- [ ] There is a video code straight after `/embed/`
- [ ] The iframe sits between `<body>` and `</body>`
- [ ] The file is saved (no white dot on the VS Code tab)
- [ ] The video actually plays when you click it in the browser

## Build and style a profile card **What you are making:** a profile card — a tidy white box on a coloured page, holding a round photograph, a name and a line about you. Team pages on real company websites are built from exactly this, and it uses most of what you have learned so far. **Time:** about 45 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. This is the biggest task so far. It comes in two halves and six stages. Do them in order, and do not skip a save. **Half 1 — build the card (in `index.html`)** **Stage 1 — the card and what is inside it** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Find the line that says `` and the line that says ``. Everything in this stage goes **between those two lines**. 3. Click at the end of a line between them and press **Enter** to make a new line. 4. Type these five lines, one under the other. The second is long — let it run off the edge of the screen: ```html

Amina Bello

I am learning to build websites.

``` `
` opens a box and `
` closes it. The three lines between them are **inside** the card, which is why they are pushed in by two spaces. The picture is fetched from the internet; if you already have a photo file sitting beside `index.html`, as in the **Images** lesson, put its name in the `src` instead. **Stage 2 — make sure the two files are connected** 5. Scroll to the top of `index.html`. Find the line that says `` and the line that says ``. 6. Look between them for a line reading exactly this: ```html ``` 7. If that line is already there, change nothing. If it is not, click at the end of the `` line, press **Enter**, and type it. 8. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. That one line is what makes `style.css` count. Without it, every word of Half 2 changes nothing at all. **Half 2 — style it (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. **Stage 3 — the page behind the card** 3. Type this: ```css body { background-color: #eef1f5; font-family: Arial, sans-serif; color: #333333; } ``` **Stage 4 — the box itself** 4. Press **Enter** twice to leave a blank line, then type this underneath: ```css .card { width: 300px; max-width: 100%; padding: 24px; border: 1px solid #cccccc; border-radius: 12px; margin: 40px auto; background-color: white; } ``` **Stage 5 — line up what is inside the card** 5. Look back at the `.card` rule you have written. Click at the **end** of the line `padding: 24px;` and press **Enter** for a new line. 6. Type these three lines. They must stay **inside** the same pair of curly brackets as the rest of the `.card` rule: ```css display: flex; flex-direction: column; align-items: center; ``` **Stage 6 — the photograph and the words** 7. Click at the very bottom of the file, press **Enter** twice, and type this: ```css .avatar { width: 120px; height: 120px; border-radius: 50%; } .card p { text-align: center; color: #666666; } ``` 8. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. The `#` is followed by six characters saying how much red, how much green and how much blue. `#ffffff` is white, `#000000` is black. Codes let you pick shades no word exists for. | | `font-family: Arial, sans-serif;` | Which lettering to use. If Arial is missing from the computer, the browser falls back to any plain `sans-serif` lettering. | | `padding: 24px;` | Space **inside** the box, between its border and its contents. This applies to `align-items: center;` and `text-align: center;` both. > Change whatever you like: the colours, the name, the words, the numbers, the picture. Four things must survive, because the checker looks for them: the `` line in `index.html`, a `color` somewhere in `style.css`, a `padding` somewhere in `style.css`, and `display: flex;` inside the `.card` rule. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. You should see a pale grey-blue page. Near the top of it, in the middle, sits a white box with rounded corners and a thin grey outline. Inside the box, from top to bottom: a **round** photograph, a name in bold underneath it, and a grey line of text under that. Everything is centred, with a comfortable band of space inside the box's edges. 5. Check the card behaves when the window is small. If the browser window fills your screen, click the **middle button of the three at the top-right corner** (between the **—** and the **✕**). *(Mac: press **Control + Command + F**.)* 6. Move the mouse pointer onto the **right-hand edge** of the window until it becomes a double-headed arrow. **Press and hold** the left mouse button and move the mouse to the **left**. 7. The card stays 300 dots wide and stays in the middle while there is room for it. Once the window is narrower than the card itself, the card shrinks with the window instead of hanging off the side — that is `max-width: 100%`. Let go of the button and drag the edge back out. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. No colour at all? Open `index.html` and look inside `` for a line reading ``. That line is what connects your two files — without it, the CSS is ignored. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Build and style a profile card" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The page is plain white and nothing is styled | `index.html` is not connected to `style.css` | Inside `` there must be `` | | The card sits against the left-hand edge of the page | The `auto` in the margin is missing | It must read `margin: 40px auto;` — `auto` is what centres it | | The photograph is a square, not a circle | `border-radius: 50%;` is not inside the `.avatar` rule | It must sit between the `{` and `}` of `.avatar`, and the picture must be as tall as it is wide | | The contents huddle against the left of the card | `center` was spelled the British way | A browser only understands `center`. `centre` is ignored | | Red cross on "lays out with flex or grid" | `display: flex;` landed outside the `.card` brackets | It must be between the `{` and `}` of `.card`. Save, then repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `index.html` has `` inside `` - [ ] `style.css` sets a `color` on `body` - [ ] `style.css` has `padding: 24px;` inside the `.card` rule - [ ] `style.css` has `display: flex;` inside the `.card` rule - [ ] `center` is spelled the American way everywhere in `style.css` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs) - [ ] The card shows in your browser as a white rounded box with a round photograph

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Now move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-hello-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-hello-YOUR_USERNAME
```

Two commands worth knowing, any time you feel lost in the terminal:

- `pwd` — press **Enter** and it tells you which folder you are in.
- `ls` — press **Enter** and it lists what is in that folder.

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it, and it means *this folder*:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens**, showing this project. Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in it.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** make a file called `hello.txt` with some words in it.

1. In VS Code, look at the file list down the left-hand side. Hover your mouse over the name of the project at the top of that list — a small row of icons appears.
2. Click the **New File** icon — it looks like a sheet of paper with a `+` on it. *(If you cannot find it, use the menu at the top instead: **File → New File**.)*
3. A box appears for the name. Type exactly:

```
hello.txt
```

and press **Enter**. Spelling matters. All lowercase, one dot, `txt` at the end.

4. The empty file opens in the big area on the right. Click in it and type anything you like — for example:

```
My name is George and this is my first assignment.
```

5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

> The words are up to you. The file must be named `hello.txt` exactly, and it must not be empty.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

1. Look at the file list on the left of VS Code. `hello.txt` should now be in it.
2. Click on another file in the list, then click back on `hello.txt`. Your words should still be there. That proves it saved.
3. If you would like to see it outside VS Code: **right-click `hello.txt`** → **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. The file is sitting in your assignment folder, like any other file on your computer.

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Your file exists on your computer, but GitHub cannot see it yet. These three commands send it up.

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add hello.txt"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed. The dot means *everything*.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot, with a short note attached so you remember what you did.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

Push often, even when you are only half finished. It costs nothing, and it means your work can never be lost.

### Step 8 — Hand it in

Pushing saves. **Submitting** is different — it asks for your work to be marked. You do that with a **tag**:

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again, and nobody is counting your attempts.

---

**That is the whole routine.** Every assignment from here follows these same nine steps. You only have to learn it once.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | The clone did not finish, or the name is wrong | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is actually there, then `cd` into the name you see |
| Red cross on "created hello.txt" | The file name is wrong | It must be `hello.txt` — all lowercase, no capitals, no space, no `.txt.txt` |

## Print a shopping receipt

**What you are making:** a small program that works out what an order costs and prints a tidy receipt into the Console, including whether the order earns free delivery. It uses everything from this module at once: variables, multiplication, a comparison and printing.

**Time:** about 40 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.
- **Your web browser** — Chrome or Edge. You will use a hidden panel inside it called the **Console**. It is one keyboard shortcut away.

---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-js-basics-project-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-js-basics-project-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-js-basics-project-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you only touch **`script.js`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** store an item, a price and a quantity; work out the total; print a receipt; and print whether the order earns free delivery.

This is the project for the module, so it is longer than the others. Take it one line at a time. Every piece of it is something you have already done.

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `script.js`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** to make a new line.
3. Type this exactly:

```javascript
// Shopping receipt
const itemName = "Notebook";
const price = 3;
let quantity = 4;

let total = price * quantity;

console.log("Item: " + itemName);
console.log("Quantity: " + quantity);
console.log("Total: " + total);
console.log("Free delivery: " + (total >= 10));
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

**What every piece is doing — read this slowly:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `// Shopping receipt` | A note for humans. JavaScript reads past it. |
| `const itemName` / `const price` | Boxes whose contents will not change in this program. |
| `let quantity` | A box whose contents might change — a shopper can want more. |
| `3` and `4` | Numbers, so no quote marks. With quote marks the maths would go wrong. |
| `price * quantity` | Multiply. The star `*` is **Shift + 8**, not the letter `x`. |
| `let total = price * quantity;` | JavaScript works out the right-hand side first, then puts the answer, `12`, into the box called `total`. |
| `"Item: " + itemName` | Here `+` joins text to the contents of a box, making one line of writing. Mind the space before the closing quote mark, so the words do not run together. |
| `total >= 10` | "Is the total 10 or more?" The answer comes back as `true` or `false`. |
| `(total >= 10)` | The extra round brackets are essential. They tell JavaScript to settle the question **first**, and only then join the answer onto the text. |

> You may change the item, the price and the quantity to anything you like. Your Total line will then show a different number, and Free delivery may show `false` — both are correct. What must stay: a `const` and a `let`, the `*` that works out the total, four `console.log` lines, and the `>=` comparison inside its own brackets.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. **Double-click `index.html`**. Your browser opens. The page may look empty — that is normal.
4. Press the **F12** key. A panel opens at the side or bottom of the browser. *(Mac: press **Command + Option + J**.)*
5. Along the top of that panel, click the tab called **Console**.
6. You should see four lines, in this order:

```
Item: Notebook
Quantity: 4
Total: 12
Free delivery: true
```

`12` is `3` multiplied by `4`, worked out by your program rather than by you. `true` is the program deciding that 12 is 10 or more.

If you chose your own item, price and quantity, the numbers will be yours — and if your total comes to less than 10, the last line reads `Free delivery: false`. That is the program working correctly.

Nothing there? Press **Ctrl + R** to reload the page while the Console is open.

Still nothing? Check that `index.html` contains `<script src="script.js"></script>` — that line is what loads your JavaScript.

Red text? Read the first line. It names the line number in `script.js` where the mistake is.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add shopping receipt script"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `Total: 34` instead of `Total: 12` | The price and quantity have quote marks round them, so they were joined as text | Write `const price = 3;` and `let quantity = 4;` with no quote marks round the numbers |
| The last line reads `Free delivery: true` when the total is small | The brackets round `(total >= 10)` are missing, so the comparison ran on the whole sentence | Write it exactly as `console.log("Free delivery: " + (total >= 10));` |
| Red `Uncaught TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.` | Something made with `const` was changed further down | `price` and `itemName` are `const` — set them once and leave them. Use `let` for anything you change |
| `Total: NaN` | `NaN` means "not a number" — one of the values in the sum is text | Check `price` and `quantity` are plain digits with no quote marks, and that both names are spelled the same above and below |
| Your code appears as writing on the page itself, and the Console stays empty | You typed the JavaScript into `index.html` instead of `script.js` | Delete those lines from `index.html`, then **click once on `script.js`** in the file list on the left and type them there |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `script.js` has at least one `const` line and at least one `let` line
- [ ] The total is worked out with `*`
- [ ] There are four `console.log` lines: item, quantity, total, free delivery
- [ ] The free delivery line contains `>=` inside its own round brackets
- [ ] Everything is in `script.js`, not in `index.html`
- [ ] The file is saved (no white dot on the VS Code tab)
- [ ] The browser Console shows all four receipt lines

assignments.name: Control Flow project: even/odd checker
assignments.description:
## Sort ten numbers into even and odd

**What you are making:** a program that counts from 1 to 10 and says, for every number, whether it is even or odd. It puts both ideas from this module to work at once: a loop to repeat, and an `if / else` to decide.

**Time:** about 40 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.
- **Your web browser** — Chrome or Edge. You will use a hidden panel inside it called the **Console**. It is one keyboard shortcut away.

---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-js-control-project-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-js-control-project-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-js-control-project-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you only touch **`script.js`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** count from 1 to 10 and print a line for each number saying whether it is even or odd.

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `script.js`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line.
3. Type this out yourself, line by line. Typing it is what makes it stick — copying it does not.

```javascript
for (let n = 1; n <= 10; n = n + 1) {
  if (n % 2 === 0) {
    console.log(n + " is even");
  } else {
    console.log(n + " is odd");
  }
}
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

**How the two ideas fit together.** The `for` loop runs ten times. Inside it, the `if / else` runs once per round and picks one of the two messages. Ten rounds, one message each, ten lines of output.

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `for (let n = 1; n <= 10; n = n + 1)` | Start `n` at 1, keep going while `n` is 10 or less, add 1 after each round. |
| `%` | The **remainder** sign. `7 % 2` is 1, because 7 divided by 2 leaves 1 over. `8 % 2` is 0, because 8 divides evenly. |
| `n % 2 === 0` | "Does dividing `n` by 2 leave nothing over?" If yes, the number is even. |
| `else` | What to do when the answer is no. |
| `n + " is even"` | Glue the number onto the words. The `+` joins them into one piece of text. |
| `" is even"` | Look closely: there is a **space** after the opening quote mark. Without it you get `4is even`. |
| `{` and `}` | Each pair marks the start and the end of a block. There are three pairs here. |

**One `=` or three? This is the line that decides everything.**

| You type | What it does |
|---|---|
| `n = 0` | **Fills the box.** It throws away the number you were checking and puts 0 in it. |
| `n === 0` | **Asks a question.** "Is `n` exactly 0?" — which is what you want. |

So the test must read `if (n % 2 === 0) {` with **three** equals signs. Write one by mistake and you get no error message at all — the output is quietly wrong, which is harder to spot. Meanwhile `let n = 1` and `n = n + 1` each use a **single** `=`, because those are filling the box, not asking about it.

**The indentation tells you where you are.** The `if` is indented two spaces because it lives inside the `for`. The `console.log` lines are indented four spaces because they live inside the `if` and the `else`. The three closing `}` brackets step back out again, one level at a time.

> **The infinite loop — how to spot it and how to escape it.**
>
> The `n = n + 1` part is what makes `n` grow, and growing is what eventually makes `n <= 10` answer no and stop the loop. Leave `n = n + 1` out and `n` stays at 1 forever, the question keeps answering yes, and the browser tab locks up: the page goes blank or grey, the Console prints nothing, and clicking does nothing at all.
>
> **To escape:** close that browser tab — click the small **✕** on the tab, along the very top of the browser window. If the whole browser is unresponsive, close the window with the **✕** in its top-right corner and open the browser again. Nothing is broken; your files on disk are untouched.

> Once it works, you may make it your own: change `10` to `20` to count further, or change the messages inside the quote marks. If you change `10`, the Console will show that many lines instead of ten. The `for`, the `if`, the `else` and both `console.log` lines must all stay.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

JavaScript does not print onto the page. It prints into the browser's **Console**, which stays hidden until you open it.

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. **Double-click `index.html`**. Your browser opens. The page will probably look empty — that is normal.
4. Press the **F12** key on your keyboard. A panel opens at the side or bottom of the browser. *(Mac: press **Command + Option + J**.)*
5. Along the top of that panel, click the tab called **Console**.
6. You should see ten lines, in this order:

```
1 is odd
2 is even
3 is odd
4 is even
5 is odd
6 is even
7 is odd
8 is even
9 is odd
10 is even
```

**Odd, even, odd, even, all the way down.** Ten lines from one `for` loop and one `if / else`. That is this whole module in six lines of code.

Check the gap between the number and the word `is`. If you see `1is odd`, the space inside the quote marks is missing.

**Is the tab frozen instead?** That is the infinite loop described in Step 5. Close the tab with its **✕**, then check that `n = n + 1` is inside the round brackets of the `for` line.

Nothing there? Press **Ctrl + R** to reload the page while the Console is open.

Still nothing? Check that `index.html` contains `<script src="script.js"></script>` — that line is what loads your JavaScript.

Red text? Read the first line. It names the line number in `script.js` where the mistake is.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add even/odd checker"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Every line says `is odd`, even for 2, 4 and 6 | The test is not comparing properly — usually one `=` where three are needed | The line must read `if (n % 2 === 0) {` with three equals signs |
| The lines read `1is odd`, with no gap | The space inside the quote marks is missing | Type `" is odd"` — quote mark, space, then the word |
| The tab freezes: blank or grey page, nothing responds | An infinite loop — the `n = n + 1` step is missing | Close the tab with its **✕**, then put `n = n + 1` back inside the `for` brackets |
| `Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected end of input` | One of the three closing `}` brackets is missing | The bottom of the file needs a `}` for the `else` and then a `}` for the `for` |
| The Console shows nothing at all | The page is not loading your JavaScript file | Check `index.html` contains `<script src="script.js"></script>` |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `script.js` contains a line beginning `for (`
- [ ] `script.js` contains `if (n % 2 === 0) {` with three equals signs
- [ ] `script.js` contains the word `else`
- [ ] There is a `console.log` line inside the `if` and another inside the `else`
- [ ] Each message has a space before the word `is`
- [ ] The file is saved (no white dot on the VS Code tab)
- [ ] The browser Console shows ten lines, alternating odd and even

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-js-data-project-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-js-data-project-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-js-data-project-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you only touch **`script.js`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** keep six scores in a list, then print five facts about them.

This is the longest piece of code you have typed. Take it one line at a time. There is no prize for rushing.

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `script.js`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line.
3. Type this exactly:

```javascript
const scores = [45, 80, 62, 90, 35, 75];

console.log("Count: " + scores.length);
console.log("Highest: " + Math.max(...scores));
console.log("Lowest: " + Math.min(...scores));

const passing = scores.filter(function (s) {
  return s >= 50;
});
console.log("Passing:", passing);

scores.forEach(function (s) {
  console.log("Score: " + s);
});
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

**What every piece is doing — read this slowly:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `const scores = [ ... ]` | The list. Six numbers, commas between them, square brackets round the lot. |
| `.length` | How many items are in the list — here, `6`. |
| `"Count: " + scores.length` | The `+` glues text and a number together into one printed line. The space before the closing quote mark is why `Count:` and `6` do not end up squashed together. |
| `Math.max(...)` and `Math.min(...)` | The largest and smallest, out of the `Math` toolbox. Capital `M`. |
| `...scores` | Three full stops, no spaces. `Math.max` wants numbers listed one by one, not a list. The three dots tip the list out onto the table for it, as if you had typed `Math.max(45, 80, 62, 90, 35, 75)`. |
| `.filter(function (s) { ... })` | Walk the list and keep only what the rule approves. `s` is a nickname for one score at a time. |
| `>=` | "Bigger than or equal to". Two characters, in that order, no space between them. A score of exactly `50` passes. |
| `console.log("Passing:", passing)` | A **comma** here, not a `+`. The comma prints two separate things side by side, and it keeps the list looking like a list. |
| `.forEach(function (s) { ... })` | Walk the list and do something with each item. Unlike `filter` it keeps nothing and hands nothing back — it runs your instruction six times. |
| `});` | The end of a `filter` or `forEach` block: `}` ends the rule, `)` closes the bracket, `;` finishes the instruction. There are two of these in this file. |

`filter` and `forEach` look alike but do different jobs. `filter` **builds a new list**, so its answer goes into a box: `const passing = ...`. `forEach` builds nothing, so it stands on its own line with no `=` in sight.

The two spaces before the inside lines are indentation. They show your eye which lines live inside the curly brackets.

> You may change the six scores to numbers of your own, and you may change the pass mark `50`. Keep `const scores = [`, `.length`, `.filter(`, `.forEach(` and every `console.log` exactly as written — the checker looks for each of them. If you change the scores, every printed number changes with them.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

JavaScript does not print onto the page. It prints into the browser's **Console**, which stays hidden until you open it.

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. **Double-click `index.html`**. Your browser opens. The page will probably look empty — that is normal.
4. Press the **F12** key on your keyboard. A panel opens at the side or bottom of the browser. *(Mac: press **Command + Option + J**.)*
5. Along the top of that panel, click the tab called **Console**.
6. You should see ten lines:

```
Count: 6
Highest: 90
Lowest: 35
Passing: (4) [80, 62, 90, 75]
Score: 45
Score: 80
Score: 62
Score: 90
Score: 35
Score: 75
```

**Read it as a report.** Six scores went in. The best was 90 and the worst was 35. Four of the six reached the pass mark of 50, and `35` and `45` did not. Then every score is listed in the order you typed it — that is `forEach` running the same instruction six times.

The `(4)` on the `Passing:` line is the browser telling you the new list holds four items. There may be a small triangle ▸ beside it; click it to open the list out.

Changed the scores or the pass mark? Then the numbers change, but you should still get ten lines in this order.

Nothing there? Press **Ctrl + R** to reload the page while the Console is open.

Still nothing? Check that `index.html` contains `<script src="script.js"></script>` — that line is what loads your JavaScript.

Red text? Read the first line. It names the line number in `script.js` where the mistake is.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add scoreboard summary script"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `Highest: NaN` | `NaN` means "not a number" — `Math.max` was handed the list itself instead of the numbers in it | Check for the three dots: `Math.max(...scores)`, with no space after them |
| `Passing: []`, an empty list | `return` is missing inside the filter rule | The line between the curly brackets must read `return s >= 50;` |
| `Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected end of input` | One of the `});` endings is missing | There are two of them — one closing `filter`, one closing `forEach` |
| `s is not defined` | The `console.log` was typed after the closing `});`, so it sits outside the `forEach` block | It belongs between the curly brackets, indented by two spaces |
| Red cross on "uses .length" | `script.js` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `script.js` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

- [ ] `script.js` has `const scores = [` with six numbers in square brackets
- [ ] The Count line uses `scores.length`
- [ ] `Math.max(...scores)` has its three full stops
- [ ] The file contains both `.filter(` and `.forEach(`
- [ ] Every printing line begins with `console.log`
- [ ] The file is saved (no white dot on the VS Code tab)
- [ ] The Console shows ten lines, starting with `Count: 6`

assignments.description:
## Build a contact card in code

**What you are making:** a small contact card: an object holding somebody's details, and a function that reads that object and hands back a tidy sentence about them. It uses every idea in this module at once — objects, functions, inputs and `return`.

**Time:** about 40 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.
- **Your web browser** — Chrome or Edge. You will use a hidden panel inside it called the **Console**. It is one keyboard shortcut away.

---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-js-objects-project-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-js-objects-project-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-js-objects-project-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you only touch **`script.js`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** store a person as an object, write a function that turns that person into a sentence, and print the sentence.

This is the project for the module. Nothing in it is new — it is the three pieces you have already met, working together. Take it one numbered step at a time.

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `script.js`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line.
3. Type this exactly:

```javascript
const person = {
  name: "Ada",
  age: 30,
  city: "London"
};

function describe(p) {
  return p.name + " is " + p.age + " and lives in " + p.city + ".";
}

console.log(describe(person));
console.log(person);
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

**What every piece is doing — read this slowly:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `const person = {` | Opens the object — one bundle holding three facts, each with a label. |
| `,` commas | Sit between the facts. The last fact, `city`, has none after it. |
| `};` | Closes the bundle and ends the instruction. |
| `function describe(p)` | Teaches the computer a trick called `describe`. |
| `(p)` | The person you hand in. `p` is a temporary nickname for whichever person is handed over — it is short so the long line below stays readable. |
| `return` | **Hands the finished sentence back** to whoever asked. Without `return` the function builds the sentence and then throws it away. |
| `p.name` | The dot means "inside". "The `name` of `p`". |
| `+` | Glues pieces of text together into one long sentence. |
| `" is "` | Notice the space before `is` and the space after it. Without those spaces the words run into each other: `Adais30`. |
| `+ "."` | Adds the full stop at the very end. |
| `describe(person)` | Uses the trick, handing over your real object. Inside the function, `p` becomes `person`. |
| `console.log(describe(person))` | Prints whatever the function handed back. |

The order matters in one way only: the object must be created before the line that describes it. Keep the three blocks in the order shown.

> Once it prints, make it yours. Add a fourth fact such as `hobby: "chess"` (remember the comma after `city: "London"`), then add `+ " and enjoys " + p.hobby` to the sentence, before the `+ "."`. You may change every name, number and place. Keep the word `return` in the function and keep the final `console.log` — the checker looks for both.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

JavaScript does not print onto the page. It prints into the browser's **Console**, which stays hidden until you open it.

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. **Double-click `index.html`**. Your browser opens. The page will probably look empty — that is normal.
4. Press the **F12** key on your keyboard. A panel opens at the side or bottom of the browser. *(Mac: press **Command + Option + J**.)*
5. Along the top of that panel, click the tab called **Console**.
6. You should see two lines:

```
Ada is 30 and lives in London.
▸ {name: 'Ada', age: 30, city: 'London'}
```

**The first line is a sentence your code built out of three separate facts.**

The second line is the object itself, and it is shown differently. When you print a whole object the Console puts a small **triangle** ▸ at the start of the line (on some browsers it is a solid ▶) and squashes the object onto one line inside curly brackets. Some browsers show even less, such as `▸ Object`.

That triangle is a button. **Click it.** The line unfolds into a tidy list, one fact per line:

```
name: "Ada"
age: 30
city: "London"
```

Click the triangle again to fold it back up. This is the Console's way of keeping long objects out of your way until you ask for them, and it is how you will inspect your data from now on.

Nothing there? Press **Ctrl + R** to reload the page while the Console is open.

Still nothing? Check that `index.html` contains `<script src="script.js"></script>` — that line is what loads your JavaScript.

Red text? Read the first line. It names the line number in `script.js` where the mistake is.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add contact card object and function"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| The first line shows `undefined` | The function has no `return` | The line inside the function must start with `return`, not `console.log` |
| The sentence reads `Adais30and lives inLondon.` | The spaces inside the quote marks are missing | It is `" is "` and `" and lives in "` — a space at both ends, inside the quotes |
| A fact shows as `undefined` in the middle of the sentence | A label is spelled differently in the object and in the function | Compare `p.city` with `city:` letter by letter, capitals included |
| `person is not defined` | The object is written below the `console.log` line, or the name differs | The `const person = {` block must come first, and the name must match in both places |
| `Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected identifier` | A comma is missing between two facts, or a `+` is missing between two pieces of text | Every fact but the last needs a `,`; every join in the sentence needs a `+` |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `script.js` has a line of the shape `const person = {` with at least three facts
- [ ] `script.js` contains the word `function`
- [ ] The function hands its sentence back with `return`
- [ ] The sentence is built from the object's facts using the dot, such as `p.name`
- [ ] There is a `console.log(describe(person));` line
- [ ] The file is saved (no white dot on the VS Code tab)
- [ ] The Console shows a full sentence, not `undefined`
