- **The second** is the hour on a 24-hour clock — a whole number from `0` to `23`.

Both come from your own computer's clock, so **yours will differ** from this example, from your classmates', and from your own run tomorrow. There is no single correct output here.

One run, made at half past two in the afternoon, looked like this — **yours will differ**:

```
2026
14
```

**How to know yours is right:** look at the clock in the corner of your screen. If it says 2:30 in the afternoon, the Console should say `14`. If it says 9:00 in the morning, the Console should say `9`. Reload with **Ctrl + R** after the hour changes and the number moves on by one.

Nothing there? Press **Ctrl + R** to reload the page while the Console is open.

Still nothing? Check that `index.html` contains `<script src="script.js"></script>` — that line is what loads your JavaScript.

Red text? Read the first line. It names the line number in `script.js` where the mistake is.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Print the current year and hour"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| The Console shows one long line such as `Wed Sep 17 2026 09:23:00 GMT+0100` | You printed `now` itself instead of a piece out of it | The two lines must be `now.getFullYear()` and `now.getHours()` |
| `date is not defined` | `Date` was typed with a small `d` | Retype the line as `let now = new Date();` with a capital `D` |
| `now.getFullYear is not a function` | The capital letters inside the name of the action are wrong | Type it exactly: `getFullYear` — lowercase `get`, capital `F`, capital `Y` |
| The hour is several hours away from your wall clock | Your computer's own clock or time zone is set differently | The Console copies your computer, not the real world — check the clock in the corner of your screen first |
| Red cross on "makes a Date" | `script.js` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `script.js` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `script.js` contains `new Date(` with a capital `D`
- [ ] There is a `console.log(now.getFullYear());` line
- [ ] There is a `console.log(now.getHours());` line
- [ ] Both action names end with their two brackets `()`
- [ ] The file is saved (no white dot on the VS Code tab)
- [ ] The Console shows a four-digit year, then a number from 0 to 23

assignments.name: Make and use an array
assignments.description:
## Keep three foods in one list

**What you are making:** a list of your favourite foods held in a single variable, with the first food and the number of foods printed out, and a fourth food added on the end. A list like this is called an **array**, and it is one of the most used tools in all of programming.

**Time:** about 30 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.
- **Your web browser** — Chrome or Edge. You will use a hidden panel inside it called the **Console**. It is one keyboard shortcut away.

---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-js-arrays-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-js-arrays-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-js-arrays-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you only touch **`script.js`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** make a list of three foods, print the first one and how many there are, then add a fourth.

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `script.js`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line.
3. Type this exactly:

```javascript
let foods = ["pizza", "mango", "rice"];

console.log(foods[0]);
console.log(foods.length);

foods.push("bread");
console.log(foods);
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

**Counting starts at ZERO. This is the part that catches everybody.**

A list numbers its items from `0`, not from `1`. Your three foods sit like this:

| Position number | Item |
|---|---|
| `0` | `"pizza"` |
| `1` | `"mango"` |
| `2` | `"rice"` |

So `foods[0]` is the **first** food, `pizza`. `foods[1]` is the second, `mango`. `foods[2]` is the third and last, `rice`. There is no `foods[3]` here — three foods run out at position `2`, and asking for `foods[3]` gives you `undefined`, which is the computer's way of saying "there is nothing there".

Counting **how many** works normally, though: `foods.length` is `3`. Only the positions start at zero. So the last item always sits at `length - 1`.

Say it out loud once, because you will need it for the rest of your life as a programmer: *the first item is at position zero.*

**What every piece is doing — read this slowly:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `[` and `]` | Square brackets. They open and close the list. |
| the commas | They separate one item from the next. There is no comma after the last item. |
| the quote marks | Each food is text, so each one gets its own pair of quote marks. |
| `foods[0]` | Square brackets **after a list's name** mean "give me the item at this position". |
| `.length` | How many items are in the list. No brackets after it — it is a fact, not an action. |
| `.push("bread")` | "Add this to the end of the list." An action, so it takes brackets, and the new food goes inside them with its own quote marks. |
| `console.log(foods)` | Prints the whole list at once, rather than one item. |

> You may use your own three foods instead of `pizza`, `mango` and `rice`, and push any fourth food you like. Keep the square brackets, the quote marks and the commas exactly where they are. Keep `foods[0]`, `foods.length` and `.push(` spelled as written — the checker looks for them.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

JavaScript does not print onto the page. It prints into the browser's **Console**, which stays hidden until you open it.

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. **Double-click `index.html`**. Your browser opens. The page will probably look empty — that is normal.
4. Press the **F12** key on your keyboard. A panel opens at the side or bottom of the browser. *(Mac: press **Command + Option + J**.)*
5. Along the top of that panel, click the tab called **Console**.
6. You should see three lines:

```
pizza
3
(4) ['pizza', 'mango', 'rice', 'bread']
```

**Line by line:** the first food, then how many foods there were, then the whole list with `bread` on the end.

The `(4)` in front of the last line is the browser telling you the list now holds four items. The browser puts its own single quote marks around each piece of text — that is how it shows text, not something you typed wrong. There may be a small triangle ▸ at the start of that line; click it to open the list out and see the positions `0`, `1`, `2`, `3` written down the side.

Used your own foods? Then the first line is your first food and the last line is your own four.

Nothing there? Press **Ctrl + R** to reload the page while the Console is open.

Still nothing? Check that `index.html` contains `<script src="script.js"></script>` — that line is what loads your JavaScript.

Red text? Read the first line. It names the line number in `script.js` where the mistake is.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Make an array of foods"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| The first line shows `mango` instead of `pizza` | You asked for `foods[1]`, which is the second item | The first item is `foods[0]` — zero, not one |
| The first line shows `undefined` | You asked for a position that does not exist, such as `foods[3]` | Three items sit at positions `0`, `1` and `2` only |
| The last line still shows only three foods | The `foods.push("bread");` line came after the last `console.log` | `push` must be on its own line **above** `console.log(foods);` |
| Red text saying `Uncaught SyntaxError` | A comma or a quote mark is missing between the foods | It must read `["pizza", "mango", "rice"]` — quote marks round each food, a comma between them |
| Red cross on "creates an array" | `script.js` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `script.js` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `script.js` has a line like `let foods = [` with square brackets after the `=`
- [ ] Three foods inside, each in quote marks, with commas between them
- [ ] There is a `console.log(foods[0]);` line — zero, not one
- [ ] There is a `console.log(foods.length);` line
- [ ] There is a `foods.push("bread");` line above the final `console.log`
- [ ] The file is saved (no white dot on the VS Code tab)
- [ ] The Console shows the first food, then `3`, then a list of four

| `function (n) { ... }` | The rule you hand to `filter`. It is a small trick, like the ones you wrote in **functions**, but it has no name because only `filter` uses it. |

| `return n > 10;` | The answer, for the item currently in `n`. `>` means "bigger than". Answer yes and the item is kept; answer no and it is dropped. |
| `});` | Three closings stacked up: `}` ends the rule, `)` closes the bracket `filter(` opened, `;` finishes the instruction. |
| `big` | The **new** list `filter` hands back. |

`filter` never changes the original. `numbers` still holds all six afterwards; `big` is a separate, shorter list.

The two spaces in front of `return` are indentation. They do nothing to the computer — they show your eye that the line lives inside the curly brackets.

Walk the rule through by hand once: `4` is not bigger than 10, so it is dropped. `12` is, so it is kept. `7` dropped. `20` kept. `3` dropped. `15` kept. Three numbers survive.

```
(3) [12, 20, 15]
```

Changed the numbers or the limit? Then a different set survives, but the shape of the line is the same.

Still nothing? Check that `index.html` contains `<script src="script.js"></script>` — that line is what loads your JavaScript.

Red text? Read the first line. It names the line number in `script.js` where the mistake is.

---

```bash

git push
```

- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

## Squeeze the repeats out of a list

**What you are making:** a list of five numbers with repeats in it, poured into a **Set** — a collection that quietly refuses duplicates — and the count printed out as `3`.

**Time:** about 20 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.
- **Your web browser** — Chrome or Edge. You will use a hidden panel inside it called the **Console**. It is one keyboard shortcut away.

---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-js-sets-maps-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-js-sets-maps-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code


- `script.js` — what it does

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** turn a list that contains repeats into a Set, then print how many items survived.

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `script.js`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line.

```javascript
const numbers = [1, 1, 2, 3, 3];

const unique = new Set(numbers);

console.log(unique.size);
console.log(unique);
```

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|

| `new` | "Make me a brand-new one of these." |
| `Set` | A collection that allows each value **once only**. It needs a **capital `S`**. |
| `new Set(numbers)` | Pour the list into a fresh Set. Anything already in there is turned away at the door. |
| `unique` | Your name for the Set. You invented it. |
| `.size` | How many items the Set holds. **No brackets** after it. |

**Why the answer is 3:** the Set takes `1`, then meets a second `1` and ignores it. It takes `2`. It takes `3`, then meets a second `3` and ignores it. Five went in; `1`, `2` and `3` came out.

5. Along the top of that panel, click the tab called **Console**.
6. You should see:

```
3
Set(3) {1, 2, 3}
```

**The first line is the count: five numbers went in and three came out.** The second line is the Set itself. The browser writes `Set(3)` to say "this is a Set holding three items", then lists them inside curly brackets. There may be a small triangle ▸ in front of it; click it to open the Set out.

Changed the numbers? Then the count is however many different values you used.

Nothing there? Press **Ctrl + R** to reload the page while the Console is open.

Still nothing? Check that `index.html` contains `<script src="script.js"></script>` — that line is what loads your JavaScript.

Red text? Read the first line. It names the line number in `script.js` where the mistake is.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Make a Set and print its size"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| The Console shows `5` instead of `3` | You counted the original list, not the Set | The line must read `console.log(unique.size);` |
| The Console shows `undefined` | `.length` was used on the Set | A Set counts with `.size`. Only lists use `.length` |
| `unique.size is not a function` | Brackets were typed after `.size` | Write `unique.size` with no `()` after it |
| `Set is not defined` | `Set` was typed with a small `s` | Retype the line as `const unique = new Set(numbers);` with a capital `S` |
| Red cross on "creates a Set or Map" | `script.js` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `script.js` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `script.js` contains `new Set(` with a capital `S`
- [ ] The list `[1, 1, 2, 3, 3]` is there, with commas between the numbers
- [ ] There is a `console.log(unique.size);` line, with no brackets after `size`
- [ ] The file is saved (no white dot on the VS Code tab)
- [ ] The Console's first line is `3`

**What you are making:** a piece of code that doubles any number you give it. This is a **function** — a trick you write once and then use as many times as you like.

**Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- [ ] The function is named `double` and takes `(n)`

## See where a variable is allowed to live

**What you are making:** a function that keeps a word to itself. You print that word from inside the function (it works), then from outside (it fails — on purpose). Where a variable lives is called its **scope**.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.
- **Your web browser** — Chrome or Edge. You will use a hidden panel inside it called the **Console**. It is one keyboard shortcut away.

---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

### Step 5 — Do the task

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `script.js`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line.

```javascript

  let message = "I live inside the function";

showMessage();
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

**What every piece is doing — read this slowly:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `function showMessage()` | Teaches the computer a trick called `showMessage`. The empty `()` means it needs nothing handed in. |
| `{` and `}` | The start and the end of the trick's instructions. Everything between them is **inside** the function. |

```
I live inside the function
Uncaught ReferenceError: message is not defined
```

The first line is black. **The second line is red, and you want it there.** At its right-hand end the Console prints `script.js` and a line number — that is the exact line the browser gave up on, the one that asked for `message` from outside the function.

Nothing there? Press **Ctrl + R** to reload the page while the Console is open.

Still nothing? Check that `index.html` contains `<script src="script.js"></script>` — that line is what loads your JavaScript.

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub


assignments.name: An arrow function
assignments.description:
## Write the same trick in one line

**What you are making:** a function written the short way, with an **arrow** `=>` instead of the word `function`. It does the same job as the functions you have already written, with far less typing — and you will see this shape everywhere in real code.

**Time:** about 20 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.
- **Your web browser** — Chrome or Edge. You will use a hidden panel inside it called the **Console**. It is one keyboard shortcut away.

---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-js-arrow-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-js-arrow-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-js-arrow-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you only touch **`script.js`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** write a function called `triple` using an arrow, then use it once and print the answer.

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `script.js`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line.
3. Type this exactly:

```javascript
const triple = (n) => n * 3;

console.log(triple(4));
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

That is the whole function — one line.

**Do not type the next block.** It is here only to look at. It is the long way of writing the very same trick, so you can see what the arrow saved you:

```javascript
function triple(n) {
  return n * 3;
}
```

Adding it to your file would give you two things called `triple`, and the browser would stop with an error.

**What every piece is doing — read this slowly:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `const` | Makes a labelled box that will not be swapped for something else later. Here the box holds a function. |
| `triple` | The name of the trick. You call it later by this name. |
| `=` | "Put what is on the right into the box on the left." One `=` sign, not two. |
| `(n)` | The number you hand in. `n` is a temporary nickname for it. |
| `=>` | The **arrow**. Type the equals sign `=` and then the greater-than sign `>`, with no space between them. It sits between the inputs and the work. |
| `n * 3` | The work. With the short form there are no `{ }` and no `return` — whatever is written after the arrow is what gets handed back. |
| `;` | Ends the instruction. This one matters: the whole function is a single statement. |
| `console.log(triple(4))` | Uses the trick with `4`, and prints what comes back. The answer will be `12`. |

`*` is the multiply sign on a computer — not the letter `x`.

> You may print a different number if you like — `triple(10)` would show `30`. The function must stay named `triple` and must keep the arrow `=>`.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

JavaScript does not print onto the page. It prints into the browser's **Console**, which stays hidden until you open it.

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. **Double-click `index.html`**. Your browser opens. The page will probably look empty — that is normal.
4. Press the **F12** key on your keyboard. A panel opens at the side or bottom of the browser. *(Mac: press **Command + Option + J**.)*
5. Along the top of that panel, click the tab called **Console**.
6. You should see:

```
12
```

**One line of code did that.**

Nothing there? Press **Ctrl + R** to reload the page while the Console is open.

Still nothing? Check that `index.html` contains `<script src="script.js"></script>` — that line is what loads your JavaScript.

Red text? Read the first line. It names the line number in `script.js` where the mistake is.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Rewrite triple as an arrow function"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| The Console shows `(n) => n * 3` instead of `12` | You printed the trick itself rather than using it | The last line must be `console.log(triple(4));` — the `(4)` is what runs it |
| `Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected token '>'` | There is a space inside the arrow, or the two characters are the wrong way round | It is `=` then `>` touching each other: `=>` |
| `triple is not defined` | The `const triple` line sits below the `console.log` line, or the name is spelled differently | The `const triple` line must come first, and the name must match in both places |
| The Console shows `NaN` | The thing handed in was text, not a number | Inside the brackets type `4` on its own — no quote marks around it |
| Red cross on "uses an arrow" | `script.js` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `script.js` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `script.js` contains the arrow `=>`
- [ ] The function is named `triple` and is stored with `const`
- [ ] There is a `console.log(triple(4));` line below it
- [ ] The file is saved (no white dot on the VS Code tab)
- [ ] The browser Console shows `12`

assignments.name: Make an object
assignments.description:
## Keep facts about one thing together

**What you are making:** an **object** — one labelled bundle holding several facts about you (your name, your age, your favourite colour). A box that holds one thing is a variable; an object is a box with named compartments.

**Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.
- **Your web browser** — Chrome or Edge. You will use a hidden panel inside it called the **Console**. It is one keyboard shortcut away.

---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-js-objects-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-js-objects-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-js-objects-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you only touch **`script.js`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** build one object that describes you, then print two facts out of it, then print the whole object.

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `script.js`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line.
3. Type this exactly:

```javascript
const me = {
  name: "Ada",
  age: 30,
  favouriteColour: "blue"
};

console.log(me.name);
console.log(me.favouriteColour);
console.log(me);
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

**What every piece is doing — read this slowly:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `const me` | Makes a labelled box called `me`. `const` means the box will not be swapped for a different one later. |
| `= {` | "What follows, between the curly brackets, goes in the box." The `{` opens the bundle. |
| `name: "Ada"` | One fact. `name` is the label (the **key**), `"Ada"` is the fact (the **value**), and the `:` joins them. |
| `,` commas | Sit between facts, like commas in a shopping list. The **last** fact needs no comma after it. |
| `}` then `;` | Closes the bundle and ends the instruction. The `;` is needed here because the whole thing is one statement. |
| `me.name` | The dot means "inside". Read it as "the `name` of `me`". This is called **dot notation**. |
| `console.log(me)` | Prints the whole bundle instead of one fact. |
| Capital letters | `favouriteColour` must be spelled the same in both places — a capital `C` in one and a small `c` in the other are two different labels to the computer. |

Indenting the three fact lines with two spaces is not required by the computer, but it makes the bundle quicker to read. Press the **Spacebar** twice at the start of each of those lines.

> Change `"Ada"`, `30` and `"blue"` to your own name, age and favourite colour. Leave the labels `name`, `age` and `favouriteColour` and the variable name `me` exactly as written — the rest of the instructions refer to them. Text goes in `"` quotes; a number does not.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

JavaScript does not print onto the page. It prints into the browser's **Console**, which stays hidden until you open it.

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. **Double-click `index.html`**. Your browser opens. The page will probably look empty — that is normal.
4. Press the **F12** key on your keyboard. A panel opens at the side or bottom of the browser. *(Mac: press **Command + Option + J**.)*
5. Along the top of that panel, click the tab called **Console**.
6. You should see three lines, something like:

```
Ada
blue
▸ {name: 'Ada', age: 30, favouriteColour: 'blue'}
```

**The third line looks different from the other two — here is what you are looking at.** When you print a whole object, the Console does not print plain text. It shows a small **triangle** ▸ at the start of the line (on some browsers it is a solid ▶), then the object squashed onto one line inside curly brackets. Some browsers show even less, such as `▸ Object`.

That triangle is a button. **Click it.** The line unfolds into a tidy list, one fact per line:

```
name: "Ada"
age: 30
favouriteColour: "blue"
```

Click the triangle again to fold it back up. Nothing is broken and nothing is missing — the Console starts objects folded because a real object can hold hundreds of facts. Opening and closing them is something you will do every day from now on.

Nothing there? Press **Ctrl + R** to reload the page while the Console is open.

Still nothing? Check that `index.html` contains `<script src="script.js"></script>` — that line is what loads your JavaScript.

Red text? Read the first line. It names the line number in `script.js` where the mistake is.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Make an object and print two parts"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| A line shows `undefined` | The label in the `console.log` is not spelled exactly like the label in the object | Compare them letter by letter, capital letters included — `favouriteColour`, not `favouritecolour` |
| `Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected identifier` | A comma is missing between two facts | Every fact except the last one ends with a `,` |
| `Cannot read properties of undefined` | The object's name and the name before the dot are different | Both must be `me`, all lowercase |
| The third line shows only `▸ Object` and you think it failed | It did not fail — the Console folds objects up | Click the small triangle at the start of that line to open it |
| Red cross on "creates an object" | `script.js` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `script.js` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `script.js` has a line of the shape `const me = {`
- [ ] The object holds three facts, with a `,` after all but the last
- [ ] There are two `console.log` lines using a dot, such as `me.name`
- [ ] There is a `console.log(me);` line for the whole object
- [ ] The file is saved (no white dot on the VS Code tab)
- [ ] The Console shows your two facts, then a folded object you can open with the triangle

assignments.name: A class blueprint
assignments.description:
## Make a blueprint, then make a cat

**What you are making:** a **class** — a blueprint for making objects. You describe what a cat is once, then stamp out as many cats as you like, each with its own name and all able to meow.

**Time:** about 30 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.
- **Your web browser** — Chrome or Edge. You will use a hidden panel inside it called the **Console**. It is one keyboard shortcut away.

---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-js-classes-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-js-classes-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-js-classes-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you only touch **`script.js`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** write a blueprint called `Cat`, then use it to make one cat and make that cat meow.

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `script.js`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line.
3. Type this exactly:

```javascript
class Cat {
  constructor(name) {
    this.name = name;
  }

  meow() {
    console.log(this.name + " says Meow");
  }
}

const whiskers = new Cat("Whiskers");
whiskers.meow();
console.log(whiskers);
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

**What every piece is doing — read this slowly:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `class Cat` | "Here is a blueprint called `Cat`." A blueprint is not a cat — it is the instructions for making one. |
| The capital `C` | Blueprints are named with a capital first letter. The checker looks for a capital letter after `new`, so **this is not optional here**. |
| `constructor(name)` | The setup instructions. They run once, at the moment a new cat is made, and they receive that cat's starting name. |
| `this.name = name` | `this` means "the cat being made right now". The line stores the name onto that particular cat, so every cat can have a different one. |
| `meow() { ... }` | An action the cat can do. Inside a class you write the name and the brackets — the word `function` is not used here. |
| `+` | Glues text together. `this.name + " says Meow"` makes one sentence out of two pieces. Note the space inside the quotes before `says`. |
| `new Cat("Whiskers")` | **Stamps out an actual cat** from the blueprint. `new` is the word that does it. The name in quotes is handed to `constructor`. |
| `const whiskers = ...` | Keeps the new cat in a labelled box so you can talk to it afterwards. |
| `whiskers.meow();` | Tells that cat to do its action. The `()` is what runs it — without them nothing happens. |

Count your curly brackets. There are three `{` and three `}`: one pair for the class, one for `constructor`, one for `meow`. The last `}` on its own line closes the class.

assignments.description:
## Turn an object into text and back

**What you are making:** an object converted into **JSON** — plain text that any computer in the world can read — and then converted back into a working object. This is how live data travels across the internet into a web page.

**Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.
- **Your web browser** — Chrome or Edge. You will use a hidden panel inside it called the **Console**. It is one keyboard shortcut away.

---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-js-json-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-js-json-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-js-json-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you only touch **`script.js`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** make an object, turn it into text, print the text, then turn the text back into an object and print one fact from it.

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `script.js`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line.
3. Type this exactly:

```javascript
const person = {
  name: "Ada",
  age: 30
};

const text = JSON.stringify(person);
console.log(text);

const backAgain = JSON.parse(text);
console.log(backAgain.name);
console.log(backAgain);
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

**What every piece is doing — read this slowly:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `const person = { ... }` | An object: one bundle holding two facts, each with a label. You built one of these in the last assignment. |
| `JSON` | Said out loud as "Jason". **All four letters are capitals.** Written any other way the browser will not recognise it. |
| `.stringify` | The dot means "inside". Read `JSON.stringify` as "JSON's stringify tool". It turns an object into **text**. |
| `(person)` | What you hand the tool — the object you want turned into text. |
| `const text = ...` | Keeps the text that comes back in a labelled box called `text`. |
| `.parse` | The opposite tool. It takes JSON text and builds a real object back out of it. |
| `backAgain.name` | The dot again — "the `name` of `backAgain`". This only works because `parse` gave you a real object, not text. |
| `;` | Ends each instruction. |

The two words worth remembering: **`JSON.stringify`** makes text to send or save, **`JSON.parse`** makes an object to use.

> You may change `"Ada"` and `30` to your own name and age. Keep the tool names `JSON.stringify` and `JSON.parse` exactly as written, capitals and all — the checker looks for them.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

JavaScript does not print onto the page. It prints into the browser's **Console**, which stays hidden until you open it.

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. **Double-click `index.html`**. Your browser opens. The page will probably look empty — that is normal.
4. Press the **F12** key on your keyboard. A panel opens at the side or bottom of the browser. *(Mac: press **Command + Option + J**.)*
5. Along the top of that panel, click the tab called **Console**.
6. You should see three lines, something like:

```
{"name":"Ada","age":30}
Ada
▸ {name: 'Ada', age: 30}
```

**Look at the first and third lines side by side — they are the point of this assignment.**

The first line is **text**. It is printed flat, with no spaces, every label wrapped in double quotes, and no triangle in front of it. That is what your object looks like once it has been flattened into something that can travel down a wire.

The third line is an **object** again. When you print a whole object the Console shows a small **triangle** ▸ at the start of the line (on some browsers it is a solid ▶) and then squashes the object onto one line inside curly brackets. Some browsers show even less, such as `▸ Object`.

That triangle is a button. **Click it.** The line unfolds into a list, one fact per line:

```
name: "Ada"
age: 30
```

Click it again to fold it away. Text has no triangle; an object does. That is the quickest way to tell which of the two you are holding.

Nothing there? Press **Ctrl + R** to reload the page while the Console is open.

Still nothing? Check that `index.html` contains `<script src="script.js"></script>` — that line is what loads your JavaScript.

Red text? Read the first line. It names the line number in `script.js` where the mistake is.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Convert an object to JSON and back"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `json is not defined` or `Json is not defined` | `JSON` was typed with small letters | All four letters are capitals: `JSON.stringify`, `JSON.parse` |
| `Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected token o in JSON` | `JSON.parse` was handed the object instead of the text | It must read `JSON.parse(text)` — `text` is the box holding the flattened version |
| The second line shows `undefined` | The label after the dot is not spelled like the label in the object | `backAgain.name` must match the `name:` label, capitals included |
| The first line shows `[object Object]` | The object was printed straight, without being flattened first | The line must be `const text = JSON.stringify(person);`, then `console.log(text);` |
| Red cross on "uses JSON" | `script.js` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `script.js` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `script.js` contains `JSON.stringify(` with all four letters capital
- [ ] `script.js` contains `JSON.parse(`
- [ ] There is a `console.log(text);` line printing the flattened text
- [ ] There is a line printing one fact, such as `console.log(backAgain.name);`
- [ ] The file is saved (no white dot on the VS Code tab)
- [ ] The Console shows `{"name":"Ada","age":30}` on the first line

assignments.name: Use a timer
assignments.description:
## Make your code run later

**What you are making:** two messages on a schedule — one that arrives two seconds after the page opens, and one that keeps arriving once a second, for as long as the page is open. Your code can now act **later**, without you.

**Time:** about 20 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.
- **Your web browser** — Chrome or Edge. You will use a hidden panel inside it called the **Console**. It is one keyboard shortcut away.

---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-js-timers-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-js-timers-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-js-timers-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you only touch **`script.js`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** print one message two seconds after the page opens, and another message once every second after that.

These two messages go to the **Console**, so this time you will not see anything on the page itself.

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `script.js`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line.
3. Type this exactly. The two spaces at the start of the middle lines are for readability — press the **space bar** twice:

```javascript
setTimeout(function () {
  console.log("Hello!");
}, 2000);

setInterval(function () {
  console.log("tick");
}, 1000);
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

**What every piece is doing — read this slowly:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `setTimeout` | "Wait, then do this **once**." Spelled as one word, with a capital T. |
| `setInterval` | "Do this **again and again**, with a wait between each time." Capital I. |
| `function () { ... }` | The instructions to run when the wait is over — not now. |
| `}, 2000);` | Three things on one line: `}` ends the function, `, 2000` is the wait, `);` ends the instruction. |
| `2000` | The wait, counted in **milliseconds**. A thousand milliseconds is one second, so `2000` is two seconds and `1000` is one. |

The wait is always in milliseconds, so multiply seconds by a thousand: half a second is `500`, five seconds is `5000`.

The `setInterval` one never stops on its own. It keeps going until you close the browser tab or reload the page. That is expected here — nothing is broken.

> You may change the words in the messages and the two numbers. The words `setTimeout` and `setInterval` must be spelled with those capital letters in the middle — `settimeout` is a different word to a computer, and will not work.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

This one prints into the browser's **Console**, which stays hidden until you open it. Nothing appears on the page.

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. **Double-click `index.html`**. Your browser opens. The page will probably look empty — that is normal.
4. Press the **F12** key on your keyboard. A panel opens at the side or bottom of the browser. *(Mac: press **Command + Option + J**.)*
5. Along the top of that panel, click the tab called **Console**.
6. Press **Ctrl + R** to reload the page with the Console open, then **watch it for five seconds**. Lines arrive one at a time:

```
tick
Hello!
tick
tick
tick
```

After one second, the first `tick`. After two seconds, `Hello!`. Then a `tick` every second, for ever. Your browser may collapse the repeats into a single `tick` line with a small number beside it that keeps climbing — that counts the same messages.

To stop it, close the browser tab.

Nothing there? Press **Ctrl + R** to reload the page while the Console is open.

Still nothing? Check that `index.html` contains `<script src="script.js"></script>` — that line is what loads your JavaScript.

Red text? Read the first line. It names the line number in `script.js` where the mistake is.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add a delayed and a repeating timer"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| The Console shows nothing at all | The page is not loading your JavaScript file | Check `index.html` contains `<script src="script.js"></script>` |
| Red text: `settimeout is not defined` | Capital letters matter in JavaScript | It is `setTimeout` with a capital T, and `setInterval` with a capital I |
| `Hello!` appears the instant the page opens | The `function () {` wrapper is missing, so the message ran straight away | The `console.log` line must sit **inside** `function () { ... }` |
| `tick` arrives far too quickly | The wait is counted in milliseconds | `1000` is one second. `100` is a tenth of a second — count the zeros |
| Red text: `Unexpected end of input` | The closing line is incomplete | Each block ends with `}, 2000);` — curly bracket, comma, number, round bracket, semicolon |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `script.js` contains `setTimeout`, with a capital T
- [ ] `script.js` contains `setInterval`, with a capital I
- [ ] Each block ends with a line shaped like `}, 2000);`
- [ ] The numbers are in milliseconds — `2000` and `1000`
- [ ] The file is saved (no white dot on the VS Code tab)
- [ ] The Console shows `Hello!` after two seconds and `tick` arriving over and over
