assignments.description:
## Split your code across two files

**What you are making:** two JavaScript files that work together — one that offers a greeting function to anybody who wants it, and one that takes it and uses it. Sharing code between files is how every real project is organised.

**Time:** about 35 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.
- **Your web browser** — Chrome or Edge. You will use a hidden panel inside it called the **Console**. It is one keyboard shortcut away.

---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-js-modules-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-js-modules-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-js-modules-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you edit **`greet.js`**, **`main.js`** and **`index.html`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** make two new JavaScript files — one that hands out a function, one that takes it and uses it — and tell `index.html` to load the second one.

Until now all your JavaScript has lived in one file. Real projects use many small files instead, each doing one job. A file keeps its code to itself unless it says **`export`**, and another file says **`import`** to take what it needs.

**Read this before you start.** When you open the finished page by double-clicking it, your browser will refuse to run it and show red text in the Console. That is not a mistake on your part — browsers are built to refuse files shared this way when a page is opened straight from your own disk. Step 6 shows you exactly what the message looks like. **The checker reads your files, not your browser**, so write the code, check the files are right, and hand it in.

---

**Part 1 — make `greet.js` (a new file)**

1. Move your mouse over the file list on the left of VS Code, on the **empty space below the last file name**.
2. **Right-click** there. A small menu appears.
3. Click **New File...**
4. A little box appears in the file list waiting for a name. Type `greet.js` and press **Enter**. The file opens, empty.
5. Type this:

```javascript
export function hello(name) {
  return "Hello, " + name + "!";
}
```

6. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `export` | "Any other file may have this." Without it, the function stays private to `greet.js` and nobody else can reach it. |
| `function hello(name)` | An ordinary function, the same as the ones you have already written. |
| `"Hello, " + name + "!"` | Sticking pieces of text together end to end. The `+` between words joins; it does not add up. Note the space after the comma inside the quotes — without it you get `Hello,Ada`. |
| `return` | Hands the finished sentence back to whoever asked. |

---

**Part 2 — make `main.js` (another new file)**

1. **Right-click** the empty space below the file names again.
2. Click **New File...**
3. Type `main.js` and press **Enter**.
4. Type this:

```javascript
import { hello } from "./greet.js";

console.log(hello("Ada"));
```

5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `import` | "Fetch something out of another file." |
| `{ hello }` | Exactly which piece you want, named inside curly brackets. The name must match the exported one letter for letter. |
| `from "./greet.js"` | Where to find it. The `./` means "in this same folder", and the `.js` is part of the file name — leave neither out. |
| `hello("Ada")` | Using the imported function, with `Ada` as the name. |
| `console.log(...)` | Printing the sentence it hands back. |

---

**Part 3 — point the page at `main.js` (in `index.html`)**

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**.
2. Look near the bottom of the file, immediately above the line `</body>`, for a line that reads `<script src="script.js"></script>`.
3. Change that line so it reads exactly:

```html
<script type="module" src="main.js"></script>
```

4. If there is no `<script>` line in the file at all, click at the end of the last line above `</body>`, press **Enter**, and type the line above.
5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `type="module"` | Tells the browser this file is allowed to `import` from others. Without it, `import` is not permitted and the browser says so. |
| `src="main.js"` | Which file to load. Only `main.js` is named here — it pulls in `greet.js` by itself. |

> You may greet a different name: `hello("Sam")` prints `Hello, Sam!`. Four things must stay: the word `export` in `greet.js`, the word `import` in `main.js`, the path `"./greet.js"`, and `type="module"` in the script line.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

**Be ready for red text on this one.** It is expected, and it is not your fault.

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. **Double-click `index.html`**. Your browser opens. The page will probably look empty — that is normal.
4. Press the **F12** key on your keyboard. A panel opens at the side or bottom of the browser. *(Mac: press **Command + Option + J**.)*
5. Along the top of that panel, click the tab called **Console**.
6. In most browsers you will see red text along these lines:

```
Access to script at 'file:///C:/Users/you/Documents/.../main.js'
from origin 'null' has been blocked by CORS policy
```

The exact wording differs between browsers; some also add `Failed to load module script`. What all of them mean is the same thing: **a page opened straight from your own disk is not allowed to load files this way.** Your code is fine. Every developer meets this message, and the ordinary fix belongs to a later part of your training — do not go and install anything to chase it now.

(If your browser happens to print `Hello, Ada!` instead, that is fine too. Some setups allow it.)

So check your work by reading your files instead. Click each one in the file list and confirm with your eyes:

- `greet.js` starts with the word `export`.
- `main.js` starts with the word `import` and the path reads `"./greet.js"`.
- `index.html` contains `<script type="module" src="main.js"></script>`.
- None of the three tabs at the top of VS Code shows a white dot.

When those four are true, hand it in. **The checker reads your files, not your browser**, so a green tick is still exactly what you should expect.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Export and import a hello function"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Red text mentioning `CORS policy` or `blocked` | Expected. A page opened straight from disk may not load module files | Nothing to fix. Check your three files by eye as Step 6 describes, then hand in |
| `Uncaught SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module` | The script line in `index.html` is missing `type="module"` | It must read `<script type="module" src="main.js"></script>` |
| `Failed to resolve module specifier "greet.js"` | The `./` at the front of the path was left out | The import must end `from "./greet.js";` — dot, slash, then the file name |
| `The requested module does not provide an export named 'hello'` | The name in the curly brackets does not match the exported function | Both must be `hello`, all lowercase, in `greet.js` and in `main.js` |
| Red cross on "uses export" | `greet.js` was created outside the assignment folder, or was not saved | It must sit in the file list beside `index.html`. Press **Ctrl + S** on every tab, then repeat Step 7 |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `greet.js` exists beside `index.html` and contains `export function hello(name)`
- [ ] `main.js` exists and contains `import { hello } from "./greet.js";`
- [ ] `main.js` calls `console.log(hello("Ada"));`
- [ ] `index.html` contains `<script type="module" src="main.js"></script>`
- [ ] All three files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs)
- [ ] You know the red CORS message in the Console is expected and are handing in anyway

assignments.name: Your first stylesheet
assignments.description:
## Give your page its own stylesheet

**What you are making:** a page whose heading has changed colour — not because you touched the heading, but because you wrote a second file called a **stylesheet** and connected it to your page. From here on, how your page *looks* lives in that file.

**Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.


---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-what-is-css-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-what-is-css-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-what-is-css-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you edit **`index.html`** and **`style.css`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** join a second file to your page, then use it to colour your heading.

This has two halves. Do them in order.

**Half 1 — connect the stylesheet (in `index.html`)**

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right.
2. Find the line that says `<head>` and the line that says `</head>`. Look at the lines between them. If one of them already reads `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">`, this half is done — go to Half 2.
3. If that line is not there, click at the end of the `<head>` line, press **Enter** to make a new line, and type this:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*.

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `<link>` | The tag that attaches another file to this page. It is a lonely tag — there is **no** `</link>`. |
| `rel="stylesheet"` | What kind of file it is: *a stylesheet*. One word, all small letters. |
| `href="style.css"` | The name of that file, spelled exactly as it appears in the VS Code file list. |

**Half 2 — write your first rule (in `style.css`)**

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. It may open completely blank — that is expected. It is an empty file waiting for you.
2. Click once in the big area on the right so a cursor blinks there.
3. Type this exactly, on three lines:

```css
h1 {
  color: crimson;
}
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `h1` | The **selector**: which thing to style. Here, every `<h1>` heading on the page. |
| `{` and `}` | The curly brackets that hold the rule. Both are required — one to open, one to close. |
| `color` | The **property**: what you want to change. Here, the colour of the writing. |
| `:` | The colon. It sits between the property and the value. |
| `crimson` | The **value**: a deep red. About 140 colour names exist. |
| `;` | The semicolon. It ends the line. Leave it out and the browser quietly ignores what comes next. |

The two spaces before `color` are only there to make it readable. The browser does not care about them, but you will.

> You may use any colour word instead of `crimson` — try `teal`, `navy` or `darkgreen`. Everything else, including `h1`, the brackets, the colon and the semicolon, must stay exactly as written.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page.
4. The big heading at the top of the page should now be deep red instead of black. Nothing else on the page changes.

Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload.

Still black? The two files are not joined. Look inside `<head>` in `index.html` for the line `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">`, and check `style.css` is spelled the same way there as it is in the VS Code file list.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Link a stylesheet and colour the h1"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| The heading is still black | The `<link>` line is missing or mistyped | Inside `<head>` it must read exactly `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">` |
| The heading is still black, and the `<link>` line looks right | `style.css` was never saved | Click the `style.css` tab at the top of VS Code and press **Ctrl + S** |
| **Every** word on the page turned red | The selector is `body`, not `h1` | Change the first line of the rule to read `h1 {` |
| Red cross on "has a CSS rule" | The rule was typed into `index.html` | Rules with `{` and `}` belong in `style.css`. Cut them out of `index.html` and paste them into `style.css` |
| The words `h1 { color: crimson; }` appear on the page as text | The rule is sitting in `index.html` | Delete it from `index.html` and type it into `style.css` instead |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `index.html` has `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">` between `<head>` and `</head>`
- [ ] `style.css` contains a rule with an opening `{` and a closing `}`
- [ ] The line inside the brackets ends with a semicolon `;`
- [ ] The colour word is spelled correctly and has no quotes around it
- [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs)
- [ ] The heading really is coloured when you open the page in your browser

assignments.name: Write a CSS rule
assignments.description:
## Learn the shape every CSS rule takes

**What you are making:** a page where all the ordinary writing is a colour and a size you chose. You do it with one rule aimed at `body` — and every CSS rule you ever write for the rest of your life has this same shape.

**Time:** about 20 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.


---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-syntax-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-syntax-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-css-syntax-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you edit **`index.html`** and **`style.css`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** write one rule with two instructions inside it, and get the punctuation right.

This has two halves. Do them in order.

**Half 1 — check the two files are joined (in `index.html`)**

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**.
2. Find the line that says `<head>` and the line that says `</head>`. Look at the lines between them. If one of them already reads `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">`, this half is done — go to Half 2.
3. If that line is not there, click at the end of the `<head>` line, press **Enter** to make a new line, and type this:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*.

Without that line your CSS file is never read, and nothing you do in Half 2 will show.

**Half 2 — write the rule (in `style.css`)**

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** to make a new line.
3. Type this exactly, on four lines:

```css
body {
  color: #333333;
  font-size: 18px;
}
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

Name the three parts out loud as you read them back:

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `body` | The **selector**. `body` means *everything on the page*. |
| `color`, `font-size` | The **properties**. What you are changing. |
| `#333333`, `18px` | The **values**. What you are changing them to. |
| `:` | A colon goes between a property and its value. Every time. |
| `;` | A semicolon ends each instruction. This is the single most common beginner mistake — miss one and the **next** line silently stops working. |
| `#333333` | A **hex code**: a colour written as a `#` and six characters. This one is a soft near-black. |
| `18px` | A size in **pixels**, the tiny dots your screen is made of. No space between the number and `px`. |

A property and its value together — `color: #333333;` — is called a **declaration**. You may put as many declarations as you like inside one pair of `{ }`.

> You may change `#333333` to any colour and `18px` to any size between `14px` and `24px`. The word `body`, the colons and the semicolons must stay exactly as written.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page.
4. The ordinary paragraphs should now be a soft near-black rather than pure black, and noticeably larger than before. Headings stay large — they have their own built-in size.

Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload.

No change at all? Look inside `<head>` in `index.html` for `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">`. That line is what lets the browser find your rule.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Set body colour and font size"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| The colour changed but the size did not | The semicolon after `#333333` is missing | Without `;` the browser throws away the line after it — add it, then reload |
| Red cross on "has a property and value" | A colon is missing | It must read `color: #333333;` — property, colon, value, semicolon |
| The headings did not get bigger | Headings are sized separately from ordinary text | Nothing is broken. `font-size` on `body` sets the size of ordinary writing only |
| The rule shows up as words on the page | It was typed into `index.html` | Delete it from `index.html` and type it into `style.css` instead |
| Nothing changed anywhere | The closing `}` is missing | A rule with no closing bracket is ignored completely — check the last line is `}` on its own |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `index.html` has a `<link>` line with `rel="stylesheet"` inside `<head>`
- [ ] `style.css` has a rule beginning `body {`
- [ ] There is a `color:` line and a `font-size:` line inside the brackets
- [ ] Each of those two lines ends with a semicolon `;`
- [ ] The rule is closed with `}` on its own line
- [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs)
- [ ] The writing on the page really has changed colour and size

assignments.name: Link an external stylesheet
assignments.description:
## Connect your two files together

**What you are making:** a page that proves your stylesheet is really attached — the moment the connection works, the whole page changes colour. One line does it, and getting that line slightly wrong is the commonest reason a beginner's styling never appears.

```bash

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.

cd webdev-css-how-to-YOUR_USERNAME

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you edit **`index.html`** and **`style.css`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** write the one line that joins `index.html` to `style.css`, then prove it worked.

Your project already has both files, side by side in the same folder — you can see them both in the file list on the left of VS Code. Sitting next to each other is not enough. You have to introduce them.

This has two halves. Do them in order.

**Half 1 — the link line (in `index.html`)**

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**.
2. Find the line that says `<head>` and the line that says `</head>`. The new line goes **between those two**.
3. If a line reading `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">` is already there, leave it alone and go to Half 2. Otherwise click at the end of the `<head>` line, press **Enter** to make a new line, and type this:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*.

The line decoded, piece by piece:

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `<link` | The tag that attaches another file to this page. |
| `rel="stylesheet"` | The **rel**ationship: *the file I am attaching is a stylesheet*. One word, all small letters, in quotes. |
| `href="style.css"` | Where that file is. Here it is right beside `index.html`, so its name alone is enough. |
| `>` | Closes the tag. There is **no** `</link>` — this tag stands alone. |

Keep `rel` before `href`, in that order, on one line.

**Half 2 — proof that it worked (in `style.css`)**

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** to make a new line.
3. Type this exactly:

```css
body {
  background: lightblue;
}
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page.
4. The whole page, edge to edge behind your writing, should now be pale blue instead of white. That colour is your proof: the browser read `index.html`, followed your `<link>` line, found `style.css`, and obeyed it.

Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload.

Still white? Read the `<link>` line one character at a time against the version above. A single wrong letter in `stylesheet` or `style.css` breaks the whole connection.

---

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash

git commit -m "Link style.css and colour the page"
git push
```

- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

git push origin submit/1
```

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```

---

### If something goes wrong

|---|---|---|

| The page stays white and `href` looks correct | The `<link>` line is outside `<head>` | Move it so it sits between the `<head>` line and the `</head>` line |
| The words `<link rel=...>` appear on the page as text | The `<` or the `>` is missing | The line must begin with `<link` and end with `>` |
| Red cross on "links external stylesheet" | `rel="stylesheet"` is missing, misspelled, or written after `href` | Write it as one small-letter word, in quotes, **before** `href` on the same line |

| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `index.html` has `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">` between `<head>` and `</head>`
- [ ] On that line, `rel="stylesheet"` comes before `href="style.css"`
- [ ] `style.css` contains a rule with an opening `{` and a closing `}`
- [ ] `style.css` and `index.html` both appear in the VS Code file list, so they are in the same folder
- [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs)
- [ ] The page really is coloured when you open it in your browser

Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are. 1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. Type `cd webdev-css-sizing-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-css-sizing-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The grey block gets slightly wider, because the 20 pixels of padding on each side are now added **on top of** the 700. Change it back to `border-box` and reload again. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. No grey block at all? Open `index.html` and look inside `` for a line reading ``. Without that line, the CSS is ignored. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Add box-sizing, max-width and image rule" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The grey block fills the whole window | `max-width` is not reaching the container | `max-width: 700px;` must be inside the `.container { }` brackets, and `index.html` must have `class="container"` | | The block is the right width but sits on the left | The centring line is missing | Add `margin: 0 auto;` inside the `.container { }` brackets | | The star rule seems to do nothing | That is correct — `box-sizing` changes how widths are counted, not how the page looks | Leave it in. The check looks for the words, and the rest of your sizing depends on it | | Red cross on "uses box-sizing" | The hyphen is missing, or the file was not saved | The line must read `box-sizing: border-box;`. Then click the `style.css` tab and press **Ctrl + S** | | The `img` rule appears to do nothing | There is no picture on this page yet | That is expected. Keep the rule — it protects any picture you add later | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `style.css` has a rule beginning `* {` containing `box-sizing: border-box;` - [ ] `style.css` has `max-width: 700px;` inside the `.container` rule - [ ] `style.css` has a rule `img { max-width: 100%; }` - [ ] `.container` also has `margin: 0 auto;` - [ ] `index.html` has `
` … `
` between `` and `` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs) - [ ] The grey column shrinks when you make the browser window narrow

Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Type `cd webdev-css-fonts-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-css-fonts-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project: - `index.html` — your web page - `style.css` — how it looks - `script.js` — what it does For this assignment you edit **`index.html`** and **`style.css`**. --- ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** choose a font for the page, make the title bigger, and push the lines of your paragraphs further apart. This has two halves. Do them in order. **Half 1 — make sure there is a long paragraph (in `index.html`)** Line spacing is the gap between one line of a paragraph and the next. A paragraph only one line long has no gaps to show you, so it needs to be long. 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. 2. Find the line that says `` and the line that says ``. What you add goes **between those two lines**. 3. Click at the end of a line between them and press **Enter** to make a new line. 4. Type this. You may write your own words instead, as long as the paragraph is long enough to wrap onto three or four lines: ```html

Typography

Typography is the choice and the arrangement of the letters on a page, and it decides how willing a person is to read what you wrote. A long paragraph like this one is the only honest way to see line spacing at work, because line spacing is the gap between one line and the next. The longer the paragraph, the clearer the change will be.

``` 5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **Half 2 — write the typography rules (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. ## Put links in a row, hide a box **What you are making:** a page where three links sit side by side like a shop menu instead of plain words in a sentence, and one paragraph that has vanished from the page altogether. Both come from a single CSS property called `display`. **Time:** about 35 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are. 1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* > **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-display-yourname`. 1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**). 2. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-display-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-css-display-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project: - `index.html` — your web page - `style.css` — how it looks - `script.js` — what it does For this assignment you edit **`index.html`** and **`style.css`**. --- ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** make three links sit side by side as grey buttons, and make one paragraph disappear from the page completely. Two words first. They run through the whole of this module, so it is worth thirty seconds now. A **container** is a box that holds other things. Picture a shoebox on a shelf. In HTML, anything you write between a tag's opening line and its closing line is **inside** that box. The things inside are its **children**. The shoebox is the container; the shoes are its children. When an instruction says "put this rule on the container", it means the outer box. When it says "the children sit in a row", it means the things inside it. Now the idea behind this task. Every single thing on a web page is secretly one of two shapes. - A **block** demands a whole line to itself and stretches across the full width available, however few words it holds. Headings, paragraphs and `
` are blocks. Think of a shelf: one item per shelf, and each shelf runs wall to wall. - An **inline** thing sits in the middle of a line of writing and is only as wide as the words in it. Links, `` and `` are inline. Think of a word in a sentence: the next word carries straight on beside it. That is the whole answer to "why is this on its own line?" — because it is a block. `display` is the property that lets you overrule which shape a thing is, and overruling it is this entire task. This has two halves. Do them in order. **Half 1 — put the things on the page (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Find the line that says `` and the line that says ``. Everything you add goes **between those two lines**. 3. Click at the end of a line between them and press **Enter** to make a new line. 4. Type this exactly: ```html
Home About Contact

You will never see this sentence.

``` 5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **What you have written:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `
` … `
` | The **container** — the shoebox. The three links live inside it. | | `` | One link, and one **child** of that container. There are three of them. | | `href="#"` | Where the link goes. A lone `#` means "nowhere yet — stay on this page". It keeps the link clickable while you have no other pages to point at. | | `class="menu-item"` | The label you will aim at from the CSS. **No dot here.** The dot only appears on the CSS side. | | The two spaces before each `` | Indenting. The computer does not need it. Your eye does — it shows at a glance what is inside the box. | **Half 2 — change the shapes (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this exactly: ```css .menu-item { display: inline-block; padding: 12px 20px; background-color: lightgrey; } .secret { display: none; } ``` 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. **What each new line does:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `display: inline-block;` | The best of both shapes. It stays in the row like an inline thing, **but** it accepts padding, width and height like a block. A plain inline link refuses to grow upwards and downwards however much padding you give it. `inline-block` obeys. | | `padding: 12px 20px;` | The cushion **inside** each link: 12 pixels above and below, 20 pixels to the left and right. `px` means **pixels**, the tiny dots a screen is made of. A bigger number means a bigger gap. | | `background-color: lightgrey;` | Grey behind each link. Without it you could not see the cushion you have added, because padding itself draws nothing at all. | | `display: none;` | Remove this thing from the page entirely. Not moved, not made see-through — **gone**, and it leaves no gap where it used to be. This is how "show more" panels and pop-ups wait out of sight until they are wanted. | | `.menu-item` and `.secret` | The dot at the front means "everything wearing this label". The names must match the HTML exactly, capital letters included. | `display: none` is worth respecting. If something you wrote has vanished for no reason you can see, a stray `display: none` is the first thing to look for. > You may change the words `Home`, `About` and `Contact`, the sentence in the hidden paragraph, and the colour word `lightgrey` — try `pink` or `lightblue`. The labels `menu-item` and `secret` must stay as they are, and the two lines `display: inline-block;` and `display: none;` must stay exactly as written. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. **Home**, **About** and **Contact** now sit side by side in a single row, each one inside its own grey rectangle, with a clear cushion of grey above, below and either side of the word. Before you wrote the CSS they were three plain blue underlined words running together in a line with no grey behind them. 5. Look underneath the three grey buttons. There is **nothing** there. The sentence *You will never see this sentence.* is not on the page, and it has left no blank gap behind it — whatever comes next has slid straight up to meet the buttons. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. Nothing changed at all? Open `index.html` and look inside `` for a line reading ``. That line is what connects your two files — without it, the CSS is ignored. Want to watch `display` do its work? In `style.css`, delete the line `display: inline-block;`, save, and reload the browser. The words stay in their row but the grey rectangles squash flat, because a plain inline link will not grow upwards or downwards. Type the line back in and save again. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Lay out a menu with display" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The three words are in a row but there is no grey behind them | The label in the HTML does not match the one in the CSS | Both must read `menu-item` — `class="menu-item"` in `index.html`, `.menu-item` in `style.css` | | Each link sits on its own line, one under the other | You typed `display: block` instead of `display: inline-block` | Change it to `display: inline-block;` and save | | The grey rectangles overlap the lines of text above and below them | You typed `display: inline`, which will not grow upwards or downwards | Change it to `display: inline-block;` and save | | The sentence *You will never see this sentence.* is still on the page | The `.secret` rule is missing its dot, or the paragraph has no `class="secret"` | Check for `.secret {` in `style.css` and `class="secret"` in `index.html` | | Red cross on "uses display" | `style.css` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `style.css` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `style.css` contains a line reading `display: inline-block;` - [ ] `style.css` contains a line reading `display: none;` - [ ] Each of the three links in `index.html` carries `class="menu-item"` — no dot - [ ] The hidden paragraph carries `class="secret"` - [ ] Every rule ends with `}` and every line inside it ends with `;` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs) - [ ] In the browser: three grey buttons in a row, and the secret sentence gone

## Pin a label to a card's corner **What you are making:** a grey card with a small red label reading **New** stuck in its top-right corner, sitting on top of the card and pushing nothing aside. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. Two words first. They run through the whole of this module, so it is worth thirty seconds now. A **container** is a box that holds other things. Picture a shoebox on a shelf. In HTML, anything you write between a tag's opening line and its closing line is **inside** that box. The things inside are its **children**. The shoebox is the container; the shoes are its children. When an instruction says "put this rule on the container", it means the outer box. When it says "the children sit in a row", it means the things inside it. **The noticeboard and the drawing pin.** Picture a cork noticeboard on a wall. You can pin a note anywhere on it and describe exactly where: *three centimetres down from the top edge, two centimetres in from the right edge*. Those two measurements only mean anything because you have agreed which board you are measuring from. CSS works in exactly that way, and it takes two lines, one on each thing: - On the **container** you write `position: relative;`. It means: *I am the board. Measure from my edges.* On its own it moves nothing. - On the **child** you write `position: absolute;` and then the measurements. It means: *lift me off the page and stick me here.* Leave out the line on the board and the pin does not fail quietly — it measures from the whole page instead, and lands in the top-right corner of the page, far from your card. That single line is what keeps the label where you want it. This has two halves. Do them in order. **Half 1 — build the card (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Find the line that says `` and the line that says ``. Everything you add goes **between those two lines**. 3. Click at the end of a line between them and press **Enter** to make a new line. 4. Type this exactly: ```html
New

Mountain bike

A strong bike for rough paths and long hills.

``` 5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **What you have written:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `
` … `
` | The **container** — the noticeboard. The label, the heading and the paragraph are all inside it. | | `New` | The **child** you are going to pin. `` is a small box that draws nothing by itself. | | `class="card"` and `class="tag"` | The two labels you will aim at from the CSS. **No dots here.** | | The two spaces before the inner lines | Indenting, so your eye can see what is inside the card. | Look at the page in the browser now if you like. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this exactly: ```css .card { position: relative; width: 300px; padding: 20px; background-color: whitesmoke; } .tag { position: absolute; top: 10px; right: 10px; background-color: crimson; color: white; padding: 4px 8px; } ``` 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. That is how a bar stays at the top of a long page. You do not need it here. > The words `Mountain bike`, the sentence, the label word `New` and the two colours are all yours to change. The labels `card` and `tag` must stay as they are, and the four lines `position: relative;`, `position: absolute;`, `top: 10px;` and `right: 10px;` must stay exactly as written. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. A pale grey card about as wide as a playing card is tall, holding the heading *Mountain bike* and a sentence below it. 5. In the **top-right corner of that grey card**, lying on top of it, a small red label reading **New** with white letters. 6. Notice what has moved. Before you wrote the CSS, the word *New* sat on a line of its own **above** the heading and pushed the heading down the page. Now it is up in the corner, and the heading has risen to the top of the card to take the space back. The label is occupying no room of its own at all — it is floating over the card. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. The label is in the corner of the **page** instead of the corner of the card? That is the missing line: `.card` needs `position: relative;`. Without it the label measured from the whole page. Nothing changed at all? Open `index.html` and look inside `` for a line reading ``. That line is what connects your two files — without it, the CSS is ignored. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Pin a tag to a card corner" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The word **New** is in the top-right corner of the whole page, nowhere near the card | `.card` is missing `position: relative;`, so the label measured from the page | Add `position: relative;` as the first line inside the `.card { }` rule and save | | The word **New** still sits on its own line above the heading | `.tag` is missing `position: absolute;`, or the `` has no `class="tag"` | Check for `position: absolute;` in the `.tag` rule, and `class="tag"` in `index.html` | | The label is in the top-**left** corner of the card | You wrote `left: 10px;` where the instructions say `right: 10px;` | Change the word `left` to `right` and save | | The label is sitting on top of the heading's words | The card has no padding, so there is no empty corner for the label to sit in | Check the `.card` rule contains `padding: 20px;` | | Red cross on "uses an offset" | `style.css` was not saved before you pushed, so `top:` and `right:` never reached GitHub | Click the `style.css` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `style.css` contains `position: relative;` inside the `.card` rule - [ ] `style.css` contains `position: absolute;` inside the `.tag` rule - [ ] `style.css` contains both `top: 10px;` and `right: 10px;` - [ ] `index.html` has a `

I am learning to build web pages. This week I found out that a picture does not have to sit on a line of its own with empty space either side of it. The instruction has a name in CSS, and the name is float. It takes two lines to write and it changes the whole feel of a page. The cure is `clear: both;` on whatever should start below the float. The picture file must be named `photo.jpg`, the labels must stay `photo` and `story`, and the line `float: left;` must stay exactly as written. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. Your photograph now sits hard against the **left-hand edge** of the page, about 200 pixels across — roughly a quarter of the window. 5. The paragraph no longer begins underneath it. Its first several lines now start **to the right of the photograph**, each line beginning a clear gap away from the picture's edge. 6. Follow the words down with your eye. The moment they pass the **bottom** of the photograph they swing back out to the full width of the page. That step in the left-hand margin is the whole effect. assignments.description:
## Give a box its own scrollbar **What you are making:** a small box holding more words than it can fit, which grows a little scrollbar of its own instead of spilling down the page — and two overlapping coloured squares where you decide which one is in front. **Time:** about 40 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are. 1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* > **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-overflow-yourname`. 1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**). 2. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-overflow-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-css-overflow-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project: - `index.html` — your web page - `style.css` — how it looks - `script.js` — what it does For this assignment you edit **`index.html`** and **`style.css`**. --- ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** two things. Make a small box keep its size and scroll its own contents. Then make two overlapping squares swap over, so the one that would be underneath comes to the front. Two words first. They run through the whole of this module, so it is worth thirty seconds now. A **container** is a box that holds other things. Picture a shoebox on a shelf. In HTML, anything you write between a tag's opening line and its closing line is **inside** that box. The things inside are its **children**. The shoebox is the container; the shoes are its children. When an instruction says "put this rule on the container", it means the outer box. When it says "the children sit in a row", it means the things inside it. **The envelope.** Picture an envelope with room for three sheets of paper. Push in six and the extra sheets stick out of the top for everyone to see. That is what a web page does by default when the words are taller than the box meant to hold them: they spill out and carry on down the page. `overflow` is the instruction that changes this. `overflow: auto;` says: keep everything inside the envelope, and give me a small handle down the side so I can slide the papers up and down. **The desk.** Now picture sheets of paper laid on a desk, overlapping. Whichever you put down last covers the ones already there. A web page does exactly the same: things written later cover things written earlier. `z-index` lets you number the sheets instead of relying on the order you dropped them. The **higher** the number, the nearer it is to your eyes. One catch, and it catches everybody: **`z-index` is ignored unless the thing also has a `position`.** A plain box cannot be reordered. This has two halves. Do them in order. **Half 1 — build the box and the squares (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Find the line that says `` and the line that says ``. Everything you add goes **between those two lines**. 3. Click at the end of a line between them and press **Enter** to make a new line. 4. Type this exactly: ```html

Monday. I made a heading and a paragraph and they both appeared in the browser, which still feels like a small miracle.

Tuesday. I learned that padding is the space inside a box and margin is the space outside it.

Wednesday. I put three links in a row and hid a paragraph with display none.

Thursday. I pinned a label to the corner of a card with position absolute.

Friday. Today I am giving a box a scrollbar of its very own.

Front
Back
``` 5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **What you have written:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `
` … `
` | The **container** — the envelope. The five diary paragraphs are its **children**. | | `
` … `
` | A second container, holding the two squares. | | `class="front"` and `class="back"` | The two squares. Read the order carefully: **`front` is written first, `back` is written second.** | That order is not an accident. Left alone, the page would put `back` on top, because things written later cover things written earlier. Your `z-index` is going to overrule that — which is exactly how you will be able to see it working. **Half 2 — control the spill and the stack (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this exactly: ```css .notes { width: 300px; height: 140px; padding: 10px; background-color: whitesmoke; overflow: auto; } .stack { position: relative; height: 180px; } .front { position: absolute; top: 20px; left: 20px; width: 120px; height: 120px; background-color: crimson; z-index: 2; } .back { position: absolute; top: 60px; left: 60px; width: 120px; height: 120px; background-color: royalblue; z-index: 1; } ``` 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. **What each new line does:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `height: 140px;` on `.notes` | The size of the envelope. **This is the line that creates the problem `overflow` solves.** Without a fixed height the box would grow to fit the words and nothing would ever spill. | | `overflow: auto;` | Keep what does not fit inside the box, and add a scrollbar only if one is needed. | | `position: relative;` on `.stack` | *I am the board.* The two squares measure from this container's edges. | | `height: 180px;` on `.stack` | An absolutely placed child takes up no room, so this container would otherwise collapse to nothing and the squares would lie on top of whatever came next. The height holds the space open. | | `top` and `left` on the squares | How far down and how far in each square starts. The second square starts 40 pixels further down and across, which is what makes them overlap. | | `z-index: 2;` and `z-index: 1;` | The layer numbers. 2 is nearer your eyes than 1, so the red square wins — even though it is written first in the HTML. | `overflow` has four values worth knowing: - `visible` — the default. The extra spills out of the box and everyone sees it. - `hidden` — chop off whatever does not fit. It is still there, but nobody can reach it. - `scroll` — always show a scrollbar, even when everything fits. - `auto` — show a scrollbar **only when one is needed**. This is nearly always the one you want, and the one you have written. > The diary sentences and the two colours are yours to change, and you may adjust the `height` of `.notes` — but keep it small enough that the words do not fit, or there will be no scrollbar to see. The labels `notes`, `stack`, `front` and `back` must stay as they are, `overflow: auto;` must stay exactly as written, and `.front` must keep the **higher** `z-index` number. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. Near the top of the page, a small pale grey box about as wide as a postcard, showing only the first two or three lines of your diary. Down its right-hand edge there is now a **thin scrollbar**. Rest your mouse over the grey box and roll the wheel: the diary slides up and down **inside** the box while the rest of the page stays perfectly still. Before you wrote the CSS, all five diary lines ran straight down the page, with no box and no scrollbar anywhere. 5. Below the grey box, two squares overlapping like two beer mats pushed together. The **red** one is in front, whole and unbroken. The **blue** one is behind it, down and to the right, with only its lower-right corner showing. 6. That is the opposite of what the page would do on its own, because `back` is written **after** `front` in your HTML. The `z-index` numbers are what brought the red square forward. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. Nothing changed at all? Open `index.html` and look inside `` for a line reading ``. That line is what connects your two files — without it, the CSS is ignored. Want proof the `z-index` is doing the work? In `style.css`, change `z-index: 2;` to `z-index: 0;`, save, and reload. The blue square jumps in front of the red one. Change it back to `2` and save again. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Add overflow scrolling and a z-index" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The diary runs down the whole page and there is no scrollbar | The `.notes` rule has no `height`, so the box grew to fit the words instead of the words being made to fit the box | Check the `.notes` rule contains `height: 140px;` | | The last diary lines are chopped off and there is no scrollbar | You typed `overflow: hidden;` instead of `overflow: auto;` | Change the word `hidden` to `auto` and save | | The blue square is in front of the red one | The `z-index` numbers are missing, or they are the wrong way round | `.front` must have the **higher** number: `z-index: 2;` on `.front`, `z-index: 1;` on `.back` | | The two squares sit one below the other and never overlap | `position: absolute;` is missing from one of them, or `.stack` has no `position: relative;` | Both `.front` and `.back` need `position: absolute;`, and `.stack` needs `position: relative;` | | Red cross on "uses overflow" | `style.css` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `style.css` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `style.css` contains a line reading `overflow: auto;` - [ ] The `.notes` rule also contains `height: 140px;` — without a height there is nothing to overflow - [ ] `.stack` has `position: relative;`, and `.front` and `.back` both have `position: absolute;` - [ ] `.front` carries the higher `z-index` number of the two - [ ] `index.html` has a `
` with five paragraphs inside it - [ ] Every rule ends with `}` and every line inside it ends with `;` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs)

Think of the top of almost any website you have visited: a strip of colour with a handful of words in a row, and each word brightening as the mouse passes over it.
