Home About Contact
``` 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **What you have written:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `
` … `
` | The **container**. It is a box like `
`, but its name tells anybody reading the page — including the software that reads pages aloud to blind people — that these links are the site's main navigation. | | `class="navbar"` | The label you will aim at from the CSS. **No dot here.** | | `Home` | One link, and one **child** of the container. | | `href="#"` | Where the link goes. A lone `#` means "nowhere yet — stay on this page". It keeps the link clickable while you have no other pages to point at. | **Half 2 — turn them into a bar (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this exactly. It is three separate rules — leave the blank lines in, they make it easier to read: ```css .navbar { display: flex; gap: 20px; background-color: #222222; padding: 14px 24px; } .navbar a { color: white; text-decoration: none; padding: 8px 12px; border-radius: 6px; } .navbar a:hover { background-color: #444444; } ``` 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. **The three rules, one at a time.** The first rule is aimed at the **container**: | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `display: flex;` | Said to the container, this means: take your children and lay them out in a row, and let me control the spacing between them. There is a whole lesson on flex ahead; for today this one line is all you need. | | `gap: 20px;` | The space **between** the children — 20 pixels between each link and the next. You write it once on the container instead of putting a margin on every child. | | `background-color: #222222;` | The colour of the bar. A colour written as a code rather than a name: this one is a very dark grey, close to black. Colour names like `white` work here too. | | `padding: 14px 24px;` | The cushion inside the bar: 14 pixels above and below the links, 24 pixels at each end. This is what gives the bar its height. | The second rule is aimed at the **children**, and its name is the important part: | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `.navbar a` | Two names with a **space** between them. In CSS, a space means **inside**. This rule finds every `` that lives inside something wearing the `navbar` label, and leaves every other link on your page completely alone. | | `color: white;` | The words themselves — white letters on the dark bar. | | `text-decoration: none;` | Takes the underline off. Links come underlined by default; in a bar the underline looks wrong, and the bar itself already makes it plain they are clickable. | | `padding: 8px 12px;` | A cushion inside each link, so the highlight has room to appear around the word and the link is comfortable to click. | | `border-radius: 6px;` | Rounds the corners of that highlight. | The third rule is aimed at a **state**: | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `:hover` | Not a thing but a moment — it means "while the mouse is resting on this". The rule switches on the instant the pointer arrives and switches off the instant it leaves. | | `a:hover` | Note there is **no space** before the colon. `a:hover` means the link while hovered. `a :hover` — with a space — means something else entirely and will not work. | > The three words may be anything you like — `Shop`, `Blog`, `About me`. The two colours are yours as well. The label must stay `navbar`, and the lines `display: flex;` and `text-decoration: none;` and the rule ending `:hover` must stay exactly as written. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. Across the **top** of your page there is now a strip of very dark grey, running the full width of the window. Sitting inside it, in a row starting from the left, the three words **Home**, **About** and **Contact** in white letters, with a clear gap between one and the next, and no underlines anywhere. 5. Everything else on your page has been pushed down to begin below the bar. Before you wrote the CSS, those three words were blue, underlined, and running together on one plain line with a single space between them and nothing behind them. 6. Now move your mouse slowly onto the word **About** and rest it there without clicking. A lighter grey rectangle with rounded corners appears behind that word alone, and vanishes the moment you move the mouse away. Try all three in turn. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. Nothing changed at all? Open `index.html` and look inside `` for a line reading ``. That line is what connects your two files — without it, the CSS is ignored. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Build a navigation bar" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The three words are stacked one above the other | `display: flex;` is missing or misspelled, so the container is not laying its children in a row | Check the `.navbar` rule contains `display: flex;` exactly, with the colon and the semicolon | | The links are still blue and underlined, and the bar has no words on it | The `.navbar a` rule is not reaching them — most often the space between the two names is missing | It must read `.navbar a {` with exactly one space. `.navbara` is a different name entirely | | Nothing happens when the mouse rests on a link | There is a space before the colon, or the rule is aimed at the bar instead of the links | It must read `.navbar a:hover {` — no space before the colon | | The bar is dark but the words cannot be seen | The words are still their default dark colour on a nearly black bar | Check the `.navbar a` rule contains `color: white;` | | Red cross on "uses flex" | `style.css` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `style.css` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `style.css` contains a line reading `display: flex;` - [ ] `style.css` contains a line reading `text-decoration: none;` - [ ] `style.css` contains a rule whose name ends `:hover` — with no space before the colon - [ ] `.navbar a` is written with exactly one space between the two names - [ ] `index.html` has a `
` with three `` links inside it - [ ] Every rule ends with `}` and every line inside it ends with `;` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs)

assignments.description:
## Put three things in a row **What you are making:** a menu strip where three words sit side by side across the page — one hard left, one in the centre, one hard right — instead of stacked one under the other. This is the shape of the top bar on nearly every website. **Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are. 1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* > **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-flexbox-yourname`. 1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**). 2. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-flexbox-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-css-flexbox-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project: - `index.html` — your web page - `style.css` — how it looks - `script.js` — what it does For this assignment you edit **`index.html`** and **`style.css`**. --- ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** make three words sit side by side in a row across the page. Before any code, one idea. The rest of this module rests on it, so read it twice. **The tray and the cups** Picture a tray with three cups standing on it. - The **tray** is the thing that holds. On a web page this is called the **container**. - The **cups** are the things being held. They are called the **children**. Now suppose you want the cups arranged in a neat row, spread to the edges of the tray. You do not walk up to each cup and give it an instruction. You give one instruction to the **tray**: *hold your cups in a row, spread out*. The tray arranges them. CSS works exactly this way. The instruction `display: flex` goes on the **container** — the tray. The children move because of it. You never put `display: flex` on a cup. In this task one big `
` holds three smaller `
` boxes. The big one is the tray. The three small ones are the cups. You style the tray, and the cups line up. **Half 1 — build the tray and the cups (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Find the line that says ``. Click at the end of that line and press **Enter** to make a new empty line under it. 3. Type this: ```html
Logo
Home
About
``` | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | The outer `
` … `
` | A plain box. Here it is the tray: it holds the three items. | | `class="menu"` | The label on the tray, so your CSS can find it. **No dot** in the HTML. | | The three inner `
` boxes | Your three cups. A `
` normally takes a whole line to itself, so right now these three words sit one under the other. That is what you are about to change. | | The two spaces starting each inner line | Indentation. It shows at a glance what is inside what. The browser ignores it; people reading your code do not. | All three inner `
` lines must sit **between** `
` and `
`. That is what makes them children of the tray. Save and look at the page now if you like: three words, stacked one per line. Then come back and do Half 2. 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **Half 2 — tell the tray to hold them in a row (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this exactly: ```css .menu { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; background-color: #eeeeee; padding: 10px; } ``` | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `.menu` | Find the thing wearing the label `menu`. The **dot at the front** means "a label", not a tag name. | | `display: flex;` | Hold your children in a row. This is the whole trick, and it goes on the tray — never on a cup. | | `justify-content: space-between;` | Spread the children along the row: first one hard left, last one hard right, the leftover space shared evenly between them. | | `background-color: #eeeeee;` | A light grey fill, so you can see where the tray is. `#eeeeee` is a colour written as a code rather than a word. | | `padding: 10px;` | A cushion of space inside the tray, 10 pixels deep, between its edge and the cups. | | `{` and `}` | The curly brackets holding the rule together. Both are required. | | `;` | Ends one instruction. Every line inside the brackets needs one. | 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. > You may change the three words `Logo`, `Home` and `About` to anything you like, and `#eeeeee` to another colour code or a colour word such as `lightgrey`. Once it works, try replacing `space-between` with `center` or `space-around` and reloading, to see what each one does. The line `display: flex;` must stay exactly as written, and the word `menu` must be spelled the same way in both files. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. The three words now sit **side by side in one row**, on a light grey strip. `Logo` is hard against the left edge of the strip, `About` is hard against the right edge, and `Home` sits between them with an even gap on either side. Without `display: flex` each word would have been on a line of its own, one under the other. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. Still stacked one per line? The `display: flex;` line is missing, misspelled, or sitting in a rule other than `.menu`. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Lay out a menu with Flexbox" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The three words are still stacked, one per line | The `display: flex` instruction is not reaching the tray | Check the CSS rule begins `.menu {` **with** a dot, and the `
` has `class="menu"` **without** a dot | | The words are in a row but bunched together on the left | `justify-content` is missing or misspelled | Add `justify-content: space-between;` inside the `.menu` rule, ending with a semicolon | | A thin grey strip appears, with the words stacked underneath it | The three inner `
` lines were typed outside the tray | They must sit between `
` and `
` — only children of the tray get arranged | | The grey strip covers the whole page and everything moved | The `.menu` rule was typed inside another rule's curly brackets | Every rule must start after the previous rule's closing `}`, not inside it | | Red cross on "uses display: flex" | `style.css` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `style.css` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `index.html` has a `
` with three `
` items inside it - [ ] `style.css` has a rule starting `.menu {` — with a dot at the front - [ ] That rule contains the line `display: flex;` - [ ] That rule contains `justify-content: space-between;` - [ ] The rule is closed with `}` and every line inside ends with `;` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs) - [ ] In the browser the three words sit in one row

## Make a row of cards that wraps **What you are making:** four cards sharing one row evenly — and dropping onto the next line by themselves when the window gets too narrow, instead of squashing into slivers. **Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are. 1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* > **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-flex-items-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-css-flex-items-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project: - `index.html` — your web page - `style.css` — how it looks - `script.js` — what it does For this assignment you edit **`index.html`** and **`style.css`**. --- ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** build four cards that share a row, and rearrange themselves when the window changes size. Same tray and cups as before. The `
` is the **tray**. Each `
` inside it is a **cup**. The difference this time: you give instructions to both. The tray is told how to run the row; the cups are told how wide they would like to be. **Half 1 — build the tray and four cups (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. 2. Find the line that says ``. Click at the end of that line and press **Enter** to make a new empty line under it. 3. Type this: ```html
Card one
Card two
Card three
Card four
``` | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `class="cards"` | The label on the tray. Note the **s** on the end. | | `class="card"` | The label on each cup. No **s**. These are two different labels, and one letter apart, so type carefully. | | Four `
` boxes with the same label | A label may be worn by as many things as you like. One CSS rule will then style all four at once. | 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **Half 2 — run the row, then size the cups (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this exactly. The blank line between the two rules is there to help you read them; the browser does not mind either way: ```css .cards { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 16px; } .card { flex: 1 1 250px; padding: 20px; background-color: #dbeafe; border-radius: 8px; } ``` **Instructions for the tray (`.cards`):** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `display: flex;` | Hold the children in a row. | | `flex-wrap: wrap;` | When the row runs out of room, let the leftover children drop onto a new line. Without this they stay on one line and squash. | | `gap: 16px;` | Leave 16 pixels of space between children, both across and down. You do not have to work out any margins yourself. | **Instructions for each cup (`.card`):** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `flex: 1 1 250px;` | Three settings in one line, separated by spaces: **grow** into spare room (`1`), **shrink** when short of room (`1`), and **aim for about 250 pixels wide** (`250px`). | | `padding: 20px;` | A cushion of space inside the card, between its edge and its text. | | `background-color: #dbeafe;` | A pale blue fill, so you can see where each card starts and ends. | | `border-radius: 8px;` | Rounds the four corners. | The `flex` line must be in the `.card` rule, not the `.cards` rule. Cups say how wide they want to be; the tray says how the row behaves. 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. > You may change the card wording, the colour code and the number in `border-radius`. Keep `display: flex;` and `flex-wrap: wrap;` in the `.cards` rule and `flex: 1 1 250px;` in the `.card` rule — those are what the checker looks for and what makes the wrapping work. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. Four pale blue cards sit **side by side in one row**, all roughly the same width, with an even gap between them and rounded corners. 5. Now drag the right-hand edge of the browser window slowly to the left, making the window narrower. The cards shrink for a while, then **Card four drops onto a second line** underneath. Keep going and they fall to two per row, then one per row. Drag the edge back to the right and they climb back up into one row. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. Cards still stacked one per line at full width? The `display: flex;` line is missing from the `.cards` rule, or the tray's label is spelled `card` instead of `cards`. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Add wrapping flex cards" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The cards are stacked one per line at any window width | `display: flex` is missing, or it landed in the `.card` rule | It belongs in `.cards` — the rule for the tray, spelled with an **s** | | The cards squash into thin slivers instead of dropping to a new line | `flex-wrap: wrap;` is missing | Add it inside the `.cards` rule, on its own line ending with a semicolon | | The cards touch each other with no space between | `gap: 16px;` is missing or was typed in the `.card` rule | `gap` only works on the tray — move it into `.cards` | | The cards are all different widths and do not fill the row | `flex: 1 1 250px;` is missing from the `.card` rule | Add it as the first line inside `.card`. Three values, separated by single spaces | | Red cross on "uses flex-wrap or flex" | `style.css` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `style.css` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `index.html` has a `
` holding four `
` boxes - [ ] `style.css` has a rule starting `.cards {` containing `display: flex;` - [ ] That same rule contains `flex-wrap: wrap;` and `gap: 16px;` - [ ] A separate rule starting `.card {` contains `flex: 1 1 250px;` - [ ] Both rules are closed with `}` and every line inside ends with `;` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs) - [ ] Narrowing the browser window makes the cards wrap onto a second line

Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-grid-yourname`. 1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**). 2. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-grid-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-css-grid-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project: - `index.html` — your web page - `style.css` — how it looks - `script.js` — what it does For this assignment you edit **`index.html`** and **`style.css`**. --- ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** lay six boxes out in a grid that picks its own number of columns. Still the tray and the cups. `
` is the **tray**; the six boxes inside are the **cups**, and you arrange them by instructing the tray. What is new is which tray you use. Flexbox arranges children along **one** line — a row. **Grid** arranges them in rows and columns **at the same time**, like eggs in an egg box. Galleries and photo walls are grid work. **Half 1 — build the tray and six cups (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. 2. Find the line that says ``. Click at the end of that line and press **Enter** to make a new empty line under it. 3. Type this: ```html
Box one
Box two
Box three
Box four
Box five
Box six
``` All six boxes sit between `
` and `
`. Only children of the tray get placed in the grid. 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **Half 2 — describe the grid (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this exactly. The long line is fiddly — type it slowly and count your brackets: ```css .gallery { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)); gap: 16px; } .box { padding: 30px; background-color: #c7d2fe; border-radius: 8px; text-align: center; } ``` | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `display: grid;` | Arrange the children in rows and columns. Goes on the tray. | | `grid-template-columns:` | Describes the columns you want. | | `repeat( … )` | "Do this as many times as it takes." The round brackets hold what is being repeated. | | `auto-fill` | "As many columns as comfortably fit." You do not name a number — the browser counts. | | `minmax(200px, 1fr)` | Each column is **at least** 200 pixels wide and **at most** one equal share of the leftover space. Two values inside round brackets, separated by a comma. | | `1fr` | A new unit: **one fraction** of the free space. Two columns of `1fr` each take half. | | `))` at the end | Two closing round brackets, because two brackets were opened — one for `repeat`, one for `minmax`. Then the semicolon. | | `gap: 16px;` | 16 pixels of space between every row and every column. | | `text-align: center;` | Puts the words in the middle of each box. | Read the long line aloud as one sentence: *make as many columns as fit, each at least 200 pixels wide, sharing the leftover space equally.* 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. > You may change the box wording, the colour code, the padding and the gap. You may also try `300px` instead of `200px` to get fewer, wider columns. Keep `display: grid;` and keep a `grid-template-columns:` line — the checker looks for both. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. Six pale blue boxes sit in a **tidy grid**: equal widths, even gaps, rounded corners, and the words centred inside each box. How many boxes sit across depends on how wide your window is — any that do not fit drop onto the row beneath, still lined up in columns. 5. Drag the right-hand edge of the browser window slowly to the left. The number of columns drops on its own, one at a time, until the six boxes end up in a single column. Drag the edge back to the right and they spread out again. Nothing in your code names a number of columns; the browser works it out from the `200px` minimum. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. One long column of boxes at full width? Either `display: grid;` is missing, or the `grid-template-columns` line has a bracket missing, which makes the browser ignore that line completely. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Add a responsive grid gallery" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The boxes sit in one tall column at any window width | The `grid-template-columns` line was ignored, usually a missing bracket | It must end `minmax(200px, 1fr));` — two closing round brackets, then a semicolon | | The boxes are stacked and nothing is coloured | `display: grid` never reached the tray | Check the rule begins `.gallery {` with a dot and the `
` has `class="gallery"` with no dot | | The boxes touch each other with no space between | `gap: 16px;` is missing or was typed in the `.box` rule | `gap` belongs on the tray — move it inside `.gallery` | | Only one box is coloured | The other five `
` boxes are missing `class="box"` | Every one of the six needs the same label, spelled the same way | | Red cross on "sets columns" | `style.css` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `style.css` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `index.html` has a `
` holding six `
` boxes - [ ] `style.css` has a rule starting `.gallery {` containing `display: grid;` - [ ] That rule contains a `grid-template-columns:` line - [ ] That line ends with two closing round brackets and a semicolon: `1fr));` - [ ] That rule contains `gap: 16px;` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs) - [ ] Narrowing the browser window changes how many boxes fit per row

## Make one box wider than the rest **What you are making:** a four-column grid where a header stretches right across the top and one feature box is twice as wide as its neighbours — the skeleton of a real page layout. **Time:** about 30 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are. 1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* > **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-grid-items-yourname`. 1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**). 2. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-grid-items-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-css-grid-items-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project: - `index.html` — your web page - `style.css` — how it looks - `script.js` — what it does For this assignment you edit **`index.html`** and **`style.css`**. --- ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** build a grid of four columns, then let two of the boxes cover more than one column each. So far every instruction went to the tray. Now some go to individual cups: *you, cover four columns; you, cover two.* The tray still decides there are four columns. The cups decide how many of those columns each of them takes up. **Half 1 — build the tray and seven cups (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. 2. Find the line that says ``. Click at the end of that line and press **Enter** to make a new empty line under it. 3. Type this: ```html
Header
Feature
One
Two
Three
Four
Five
``` Look closely at the second and third lines. They each carry **two labels**, separated by a single space: | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `class="box"` | One label. This box is an ordinary box. | | `class="box header"` | **Two** labels on one thing: it is a box **and** it is the header. Separate them with one space, inside the same pair of quote marks. | | Why bother | The `box` label gives it the same padding and colour as the others. The `header` label is what you aim the "stretch across the top" instruction at. Each label does one job. | 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **Half 2 — four columns, then two exceptions (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this exactly, all four rules, in this order: ```css .layout { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr); gap: 16px; } .box { padding: 20px; background-color: #fde68a; border-radius: 8px; text-align: center; } .header { grid-column: span 4; } .feature { grid-column: span 2; } ``` | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `repeat(4, 1fr)` | Four columns, each one equal share wide. The `4` is a count; the comma separates it from the width. | | `grid-column: span 4;` | This cup covers **4** columns instead of 1. On a four-column grid, that is the full width. | | `grid-column: span 2;` | This cup covers **2** columns — twice as wide as an ordinary one. | | `span` | The word is part of the instruction here. It has nothing to do with the `` tag. | | Why `.header` comes after `.box` | Both rules apply to the header box. They set different things, so they do not argue; the box gets its padding and colour from one and its width from the other. | 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. > You may change the wording inside the boxes, the colour code and the padding. You may also give one box `grid-row: span 2;` to make it two rows tall. Keep `display: grid;`, keep `repeat(4, 1fr)`, and keep at least one `grid-column:` line — the checker looks for a `grid-column` or `grid-row` instruction. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. You should see three rows of yellow boxes: - **Row one:** the box marked *Header*, stretched across the **full width** of the page on its own. - **Row two:** *Feature* on the left, **twice as wide** as the boxes beside it, then *One* and *Two*. - **Row three:** *Three*, *Four* and *Five*, each one column wide, with an empty space where a fourth would go. 5. All the gaps between boxes are even, and every box has the same yellow fill and rounded corners. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. Every box the same width? The `grid-column` lines are not landing — check the two-label spelling `class="box header"` in the HTML against `.header` in the CSS. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Span grid items across columns" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | *Header* sits in one column like all the others | The `header` label is missing or misspelled in one of the two files | The HTML needs `class="box header"` (one space, no dot) and the CSS needs `.header {` (with a dot) | | *Header* stretches across, but has no yellow fill or padding | The word `box` was left off that `
` | It must carry both labels: `class="box header"` | | All seven boxes sit in one tall column | `display: grid;` or the `grid-template-columns` line is missing from `.layout` | Both belong inside the `.layout` rule, each ending with a semicolon | | There are more or fewer than four columns | The number in `repeat(4, 1fr)` was mistyped | It reads `repeat(4, 1fr)` — a `4`, a comma, then `1fr`, with one closing bracket | | Red cross on "spans an item" | The property was typed without its hyphen, or `style.css` was not saved | It is `grid-column`, not `gridcolumn`. Then press **Ctrl + S** and repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `index.html` has a `
` holding seven boxes - [ ] One box carries `class="box header"` and one carries `class="box feature"` - [ ] `style.css` has `.layout {` containing `display: grid;` and `grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);` - [ ] There is a `.header` rule containing `grid-column: span 4;` - [ ] There is a `.feature` rule containing `grid-column: span 2;` - [ ] Every rule is closed with `}` and every line inside ends with `;` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs)

assignments.name: Layout project: card gallery
assignments.description: ## Build a card gallery that reflows **What you are making:** a finished gallery page — a heading and four cards, each with a coloured top strip, a title and a line of text — laid out in a grid that changes how many cards it puts per row as the window changes size. This is the layout real shop and portfolio sites use. **Time:** about 45 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are. 1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* > **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-layout-project-yourname`. 1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**). 2. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-layout-project-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-css-layout-project-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project: - `index.html` — your web page - `style.css` — how it looks - `script.js` — what it does For this assignment you edit **`index.html`** and **`style.css`**. --- ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** build a complete page — a heading and four cards in a grid — that rearranges itself as the window changes width. This one is longer than the others in this module, so it is split into six stages. Do them in order and save as you go. Nothing here is new: it is the tray and the cups, the grid, and the card styling you have already met, put together into one page. --- **Half 1 — build the page (in `index.html`)** **Stage 1 — connect your two files** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. 2. Look near the top of the file, between `` and ``, for a line that reads: ```html ``` 3. If that line is already there, change nothing and go to Stage 2. If it is not there, click at the end of the `` line, press **Enter**, and type it in. That single line is what makes `style.css` affect this page. Without it your styling is written but never used, and the checker will mark it as missing. **Stage 2 — clear the old content out of the body** 1. Find the line that says `<body>` and the line that says `</body>`. 2. Click at the very start of the first line **below** `<body>`, hold the **Shift** key down, and click at the very end of the last line **above** `</body>`. Everything between turns blue. 3. Press **Backspace** *(the key above Enter, sometimes marked ←)*. 4. Leave `<body>` and `</body>` themselves alone. If you deleted one by accident, type it back. **Stage 3 — type the heading and the four cards** 1. Put the blinking line between `<body>` and `</body>`. 2. Type this. It is repetitive on purpose — the four cards are identical apart from their words: ```html <h1>My Gallery</h1> <div class="gallery"> <div class="card"> <div class="card-top"></div> <h2>First card</h2> <p>A short line about this card.</p> </div> <div class="card"> <div class="card-top"></div> <h2>Second card</h2> <p>A short line about this card.</p> </div> <div class="card"> <div class="card-top"></div> <h2>Third card</h2> <p>A short line about this card.</p> </div> <div class="card"> <div class="card-top"></div> <h2>Fourth card</h2> <p>A short line about this card.</p> </div> </div> ``` | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `<div class="gallery">` | The tray. It holds the four cards. | | `<div class="card">` | One cup — and itself a small tray, because it holds three things of its own. Trays inside trays is ordinary and expected. | | `<div class="card-top"></div>` | An opening tag and a closing tag with **nothing between them**: an empty box. It exists only so you can give it a height and a colour and get a coloured strip. | | The hyphen in `card-top` | Part of the name. A label may contain hyphens; it may not contain spaces. | 3. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. --- **Half 2 — style the page (in `style.css`)** In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. Stages 4, 5 and 6 are typed one after another, down the same file. **Stage 4 — settle the page itself** 1. Type this: ```css * { box-sizing: border-box; } body { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; background-color: #f4f4f4; padding: 20px; } ``` | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `*` | A star means **every single thing on the page**. No dot, no name. | | `box-sizing: border-box;` | Tells the browser to count padding and borders **inside** a box's stated width, not on top of it. Without it, widths creep past what you asked for. Put this line in every project. | | `font-family: Arial, sans-serif;` | Use Arial; if the computer has no Arial, use any plain typeface. The comma offers an alternative. | | `padding: 20px;` | A cushion round the whole page, so nothing touches the window edge. | **Stage 5 — make the gallery a responsive grid** 1. Press **Enter** twice to leave a blank line, then type this: ```css .gallery { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)); gap: 16px; } ``` This is the same recipe you used for the box gallery: *as many columns as fit, each at least 200 pixels wide, sharing the leftover space equally*, with 16 pixels of space between every row and column. Count the closing brackets: `1fr));`. **Stage 6 — style the cards** 1. Press **Enter** twice again, then type this: ```css .card { background-color: white; border: 1px solid #dddddd; border-radius: 8px; padding: 20px; } .card-top { height: 60px; border-radius: 4px; background-color: #60a5fa; margin-bottom: 12px; } ``` | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `border: 1px solid #dddddd;` | Three values in one line, separated by spaces: how thick, what kind of line, what colour. | | `border-radius: 8px;` | Rounds the corners of the card. | | `padding: 20px;` | Space inside the card, between its edge and its contents. | | `height: 60px;` | Forces the empty top box to be 60 pixels tall. An empty box with no height is invisible, which is why this line matters. | | `margin-bottom: 12px;` | Space **outside** the top strip, below it — pushing the title down. Padding is inside a box; margin is outside it. | 2. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. > Change the heading, the card titles and the sentences to whatever you like, and pick your own colour codes. If you would like to go further, add `box-shadow: 0 2px 6px #cccccc;` inside the `.card` rule for a soft shadow. Four things must stay: the `<link>` line in `index.html`, `display: grid;`, the `gap:` line, and the `padding`, `border` and `background-color` lines on `.card`. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. At the top, **My Gallery** in large letters. Below it, four white cards on a light grey page. Each card has a **blue strip across its top**, a title underneath, and a line of text below that. The cards have thin grey borders and rounded corners, with even gaps between them. 5. assignments.description:
## Store a colour once, use it everywhere

**What you are making:** a page whose colour and spacing are written down in **one** place at the top of your CSS. Change that one line and the whole page changes at once.

**Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.


---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-variables-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-variables-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-css-variables-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you edit **`index.html`** and **`style.css`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** write a colour and a spacing size once, give each a name, then use those names in two different rules.

This has two halves. Do them in order.

**Half 1 — add a button to style (in `index.html`)**

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right.
2. Find the line that reads `</body>`. It is near the bottom.
3. Click at the end of the line **above** `</body>` and press **Enter** to make a new empty line.
4. Type this exactly:

```html
<button class="brand-button">Get in touch</button>
```

5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*.

**Half 2 — write the names, then use them (in `style.css`)**

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line.
3. Type this exactly:

```css
:root {
  --brand: #6a11cb;
  --space: 16px;
}

body {
  color: var(--brand);
  padding: var(--space);
}

.brand-button {
  background-color: var(--brand);
  color: white;
  border: none;
  padding: var(--space);
  font-size: 16px;
}
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

**The new pieces:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `:root` | Stands for the whole page. Names written here can be used by every rule in the file. |
| `--brand` | A name **you** invented. Any name you like, so long as it starts with **two dashes**. The two dashes are what tell CSS "this is a stored value, not a real property". |
| `--brand: #6a11cb;` | Stores the colour under that name. On its own it changes nothing on screen. |
| `var(--brand)` | Fetches the stored value back out. Wherever you write this, CSS puts `#6a11cb`. |
| `#6a11cb` | A colour written as a code: a `#` and six characters. This one is purple. |
| `16px` | Sixteen pixels — a length. A pixel is one dot on your screen. |
| `padding` | Empty breathing space **inside** the edge of the thing. |

The point is not that it looks nice. The point is that the purple now lives in **one** line. You will prove that in Step 6.

> You may use any colour code you like after `--brand:`, and any size after `--space:`. The names `--brand`, `--space` and the `var(...)` wrapping must stay exactly as written.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page.
4. All of the writing on the page should now be purple, the page should have a band of empty space round its edge, and the `Get in touch` button should be a solid purple block with white writing on it.

Now prove why variables are worth having:

5. Go back to VS Code, click the `style.css` tab, and change the one line `--brand: #6a11cb;` to read `--brand: #b3261e;` instead.
6. Press **Ctrl + S** to save, click back to the browser, and press **Ctrl + R** to reload.
7. The writing **and** the button turn red together. You changed one line and two rules followed. That is the whole point. Leave it red or put the purple back — either passes.

Nothing is coloured at all? Open `index.html` and look inside `<head>` for a line reading `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">`. That line is what connects your two files — without it, the CSS is ignored.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add CSS variables for colour and space"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Nothing is purple, everything looks plain | The name is spelled differently in the two places | `--brand` in `:root` and `var(--brand)` must match letter for letter, including the two dashes |
| Nothing is purple, everything looks plain | One dash instead of two | It must be `--brand`, not `-brand`. Two dashes at the front, both times |
| Red cross on "uses var()" | The `var(` wrapper is missing | `color: --brand;` does not work. It must read `color: var(--brand);` |
| Red cross on "defines a variable" | The `:root` block is missing or has no colon | `:root` needs a line inside it shaped like `--brand: #6a11cb;` — name, colon, value, semicolon |
| The button is purple but the writing is not | The `body` rule was left out | Both rules are needed. The check wants `var(--` used, and the point of the task is using it more than once |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `style.css` has a `:root` block containing `--brand: #6a11cb;` and `--space: 16px;`
- [ ] Each stored name starts with **two** dashes
- [ ] `var(--brand)` is used in at least two different rules
- [ ] `index.html` has the `<button class="brand-button">` line
- [ ] Every line inside the curly brackets ends with `;`
- [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs)
- [ ] Changing the one `--brand` line changes both the writing and the button

assignments.name: Transitions
assignments.description:
## Make a button change slowly, not instantly

**What you are making:** a button that eases from purple to blue and slides gently upwards when you point at it, instead of snapping. One line of CSS is the difference between a page that feels cheap and one that feels finished.

**Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.


---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-transitions-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-transitions-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-css-transitions-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project:

- `index.html` — your web page
- `style.css` — how it looks
- `script.js` — what it does

For this assignment you edit **`index.html`** and **`style.css`**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** make a button's hover change happen smoothly over a fifth of a second.

This has two halves. Do them in order.

**Half 1 — put the button on the page (in `index.html`)**

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right.
2. Find the line that reads `</body>`. It is near the bottom.
3. Click at the end of the line **above** `</body>` and press **Enter** to make a new empty line.
4. Type this exactly:

```html
<button class="btn">Hover over me</button>
```

5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*.

**Half 2 — make the change smooth (in `style.css`)**

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line.
3. Type this exactly:

```css
.btn {
  background-color: #6a11cb;
  color: white;
  border: none;
  padding: 12px 24px;
  border-radius: 8px;
  font-size: 16px;
  transition: all 0.2s ease;
}

.btn:hover {
  background-color: #2575fc;
  transform: translateY(-4px);
}
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

**The new pieces:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `transition` | "Do not switch straight to the new look — travel to it." It goes on the **normal** rule, never on the `:hover` rule. This catches people out every time. |
| `all` | Which changes to travel through. `all` means every one of them. |
| `0.2s` | How long the journey takes. `s` means seconds, so this is two tenths of a second. |
| `ease` | The style of the journey: starts gently, speeds up, slows down at the end. |
| `transform: translateY(-4px);` | Move this thing. `translateY` means up and down, and **the minus sign means upwards**. Four pixels up. Nothing around it shifts to make room. |
| `padding: 12px 24px;` | Two measurements: 12 pixels of space above and below, 24 to the left and right. |

Read the two rules together. The `.btn` rule says what the button normally looks like *and how it travels*. The `.btn:hover` rule says where it travels **to**.

> You may change the two colour codes and the button's words. Keep the `transition` line on the `.btn` rule and the `:hover` on the second rule.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page.
4. You should see a purple button with rounded corners and white writing.
5. Now **move your mouse pointer on top of the button and leave it there**. Do not click. The purple does not switch to blue — it *fades* into blue, and the button glides about four pixels upwards at the same time. It takes about a fifth of a second.
6. **Move the pointer away.** It fades and glides back down, as smoothly as before.

If that felt too quick to be sure of, slow it right down:

7. Go back to VS Code, click the `style.css` tab, and change `0.2s` to `2s`.
8. Press **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser, press **Ctrl + R** to reload, then point at the button again. Now the journey takes two full seconds and you can watch the colour crawl across. Put `0.2s` back afterwards — two seconds is far too slow for a real page.

The colour snaps instead of fading? The `transition` line is on the wrong rule. It belongs in `.btn`, not `.btn:hover`.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add a smooth hover transition"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| The colour changes, but it snaps instantly | The `transition` line is inside the `:hover` rule | Move it up into the plain `.btn` rule. The transition lives on the normal state |
| Nothing happens at all when you point at it | The two rules use different names | `.btn` and `.btn:hover` must match, and the button must read `<button class="btn">` |
| The button moves down instead of up | The minus sign is missing | It is `translateY(-4px)`. Without the minus it travels downwards |
| Red cross on "uses transition" | The word is misspelled or the colon is missing | The line reads `transition: all 0.2s ease;` — word, colon, three values, semicolon |
| The button jumps around and pushes other things aside | `margin-top` was used instead of `transform` | `transform` moves the button without disturbing anything else. Use the line as written |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `style.css` contains `transition: all 0.2s ease;` inside the plain `.btn` rule
- [ ] `style.css` contains a `.btn:hover` rule
- [ ] The `:hover` rule changes the background colour and has `transform: translateY(-4px);`
- [ ] `index.html` has the `<button class="btn">` line
- [ ] Every line inside the curly brackets ends with `;`
- [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs)
- [ ] Pointing at the button makes it fade and glide rather than snap

Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. Welcome

``` 5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. A `

The window is shorter — and the blue band is shorter with it, still filling it exactly. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. No blue band at all? Open `index.html` and look inside `` for a line reading ``. That line is what connects your two files — without it, the CSS is ignored. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Size with rem, percent and vh" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The blue band is only as tall as the word inside it | `height: 100vh;` landed in the wrong rule | It must sit between the `{` and `}` of `.hero` | | The heading is its ordinary size | The names do not match | `class="title"` in the HTML, `.title` in the CSS — same spelling, and only the CSS gets a dot | | None of the three sizes took effect | A space crept in between a number and its unit | Write `3rem`, `50%` and `100vh` — never `3 rem` | | The column runs the full width of the page | The `%` sign is missing | `width: 50;` means nothing to a browser. It must read `width: 50%;` | | Red cross on "uses rem, vh or vw" | `style.css` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `style.css` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `style.css` has a `font-size` written in `rem`, such as `3rem` - [ ] `style.css` has `height: 100vh;` inside the `.hero` rule - [ ] `style.css` has a `width` written with a `%` - [ ] No number has a space between it and its unit - [ ] `title`, `column` and `hero` are spelled the same in both files - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs) - [ ] The blue band fills your browser window from top to bottom
