## Stack your columns on a narrow screen **What you are making:** a page with two boxes side by side that drop into a single stack when the window gets narrow. One page, two shapes — this is how a website fits a laptop and a phone at the same time. **Time:** about 30 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-media-queries-yourname`. 1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**). 2. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-media-queries-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-css-media-queries-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project: - `index.html` — your web page - `style.css` — how it looks - `script.js` — what it does For this assignment you edit **`index.html`** and **`style.css`**. --- ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** put two boxes side by side, then tell the browser to stack them whenever there is not enough room. This has two halves. Do them in order. **Half 1 — make the two boxes (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Near the top of the file, find the line that says ``. Click at the end of that line and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this one line. It is long — let it run off the edge of the screen and do not press **Enter** in the middle of it: ```html ``` That line tells a phone to admit how wide it really is. Without it, a phone pretends to be a wide desktop and everything else in this task is ignored on the very devices it was written for. 4. Now find the line that says `` and the line that says ``. Click at the end of a line between them and press **Enter**. 5. Type these four lines, one under the other: ```html
Column one
Column two
``` 6. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. The outer box is labelled `layout`. The two boxes inside it are both labelled `box` — a class may be used as many times as you like on one page. **Half 2 — the wide rule, then the narrow rule (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this exactly. Mind the brackets near the end — there are three closing brackets, and every one is needed: ```css .layout { display: flex; gap: 20px; } .box { width: 50%; padding: 20px; background-color: lightblue; } @media (max-width: 700px) { .layout { flex-direction: column; } .box { width: 100%; } } ``` 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. **What each piece means:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `display: flex;` | Lays the boxes inside `.layout` out in a row, side by side. | | `gap: 20px;` | A 20-dot space between them. | | `@media` | "Only under certain conditions." Every rule inside it is switched off until the condition is true. | | `(max-width: 700px)` | The condition: the window is **at most** 700 dots wide. Read it as "while the window is 700 dots or narrower". | | `flex-direction: column;` | Turns that row into a stack, one box above the other. | | `width: 100%;` | Once stacked, each box takes the full width rather than half of it. | **About the brackets.** `@media` has a pair of curly brackets of its own, and each rule inside has its own pair as well. So the end of the file has three `}` in a row, each on its own line, stepping back towards the left. Leave one out and the browser discards the whole block without a word of complaint. > You may change the words inside the boxes, the colour, and the number `700`. `@media`, `max-width` and `flex-direction: column;` must stay exactly as written. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. You should see two light blue boxes **side by side**, with a gap between them. A media query only shows what it does when the window **changes size**. So now change the size of the window by hand. 5. Look at the **top-right corner** of the browser window. There are three small buttons: **—**, a square, and **✕**. Click the **middle** one. The window shrinks away from the edges of the screen, so there is now room to pull it about. *(Mac: if the window fills the screen, press **Control + Command + F** first.)* 6. Move the mouse pointer slowly onto the **right-hand edge** of the browser window — the very border, where the window stops. The pointer changes shape into a double-headed arrow. That shape means "this edge can be dragged". 7. **Press and hold** the left mouse button. Do not let go yet. 8. Still holding, move the mouse steadily to the **left**. The window gets narrower as you go. 9. Keep watching the two blue boxes while you drag. At the moment the window becomes narrower than 700 dots the boxes **jump**. You cannot see that number anywhere, so drag slowly and watch for the change: instead of sitting side by side they are now one above the other, each one running the full width. 10. Let go of the mouse button. Then drag that same edge back out to the right. The boxes hop back into a row. That jump is your media query switching on and off. Nothing reloaded and nothing was retyped — the same page carries two shapes at once. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. They never stack, however narrow you drag? Count the closing brackets at the bottom of `style.css` — there must be three. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Stack columns on narrow screens" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The boxes never stack, however narrow the window | A closing bracket is missing, so the browser discarded the media query | `style.css` must end with three `}` lines, one under the other | | The boxes are stacked even when the window is wide | You typed `min-width` where the task says `max-width` | `max-width` means "at most this wide" — change it back | | The boxes are one above the other from the very start | `.layout` has no `display: flex;` | Add `display: flex;` inside the `.layout` rule, above the media query | | The window will not get any narrower | The window is maximised — pinned to the edges of the screen | Click the **middle button of the three** at the top-right corner first, then drag the edge | | Red cross on "uses a media query" | The `@` is missing, or `style.css` was not saved | The line must begin `@media`. Press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `style.css` contains a line beginning `@media` - [ ] The condition on that line reads `(max-width: 700px)` - [ ] `.layout` has `display: flex;` - [ ] Inside the media query, `.layout` has `flex-direction: column;` - [ ] `style.css` ends with three `}` lines, one under the other - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs) - [ ] You have dragged the window narrow and watched the boxes stack

Keep `max-width: 100%;` inside the `img` rule exactly as written. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. You should see your heading in its ordinary dark colour and, underneath it, a photograph that stops neatly at the edge of the page rather than running off it. Both of the things you wrote only show themselves when the window **changes size**. So now change the size of the window by hand. 5. Look at the **top-right corner** of the browser window. There are three small buttons: **—**, a square, and **✕**. Click the **middle** one. The window shrinks away from the edges of the screen, so there is now room to pull it about. *(Mac: if the window fills the screen, press **Control + Command + F** first.)* 6. Move the mouse pointer slowly onto the **right-hand edge** of the browser window — the very border. The pointer changes shape into a double-headed arrow. That shape means "this edge can be dragged". 7. **Press and hold** the left mouse button, and while holding it, move the mouse steadily to the **left**. The window gets narrower as you go. Do not let go yet. 8. Watch the photograph. It narrows along with the window and stays inside it. Without `max-width: 100%` it would keep its 1200 dots and push a scroll bar along the bottom of the page. 9. Keep going. Once the window is narrower than 600 dots — roughly a third of your screen — the heading turns **crimson**. That is the media query switching on. 10. Let go of the mouse button, then drag the same edge back out to the right. The heading returns to its ordinary colour and the photograph grows again, up to 1200 dots and no further. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. A broken picture icon instead of a photograph? The picture comes from the internet, so this page needs a connection. The heading colour still works without one. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Make the page fit small screens" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | A broken picture icon instead of a photograph | The picture is fetched from the internet and you are not connected | Connect, then press **Ctrl + R**. The heading colour part of the task works without a connection | | A scroll bar appears along the bottom and the picture runs off the side | The `img` rule is missing or misspelt | It must read `img { max-width: 100%; }` — `max-width`, with the hyphen | | The heading never changes colour, however narrow the window | A closing bracket is missing at the end of the media query | `style.css` must end with two `}` lines, one under the other | | The heading is crimson even on a wide window | The colour rule is sitting outside the media query | The `.headline` rule must be **between** the `{` and `}` that belong to `@media` | | The window will not get any narrower | The window is maximised — pinned to the edges of the screen | Click the **middle button of the three** at the top-right corner first, then drag the edge | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `style.css` has an `img` rule containing `max-width: 100%;` - [ ] `style.css` contains a line beginning `@media` - [ ] The condition on that line reads `(max-width: 600px)` - [ ] A `color` is set on `.headline` inside the media query - [ ] `style.css` ends with two `}` lines, one under the other - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs) - [ ] You have dragged the window narrow and watched the heading change colour

assignments.name: Specificity & the cascade
assignments.description:
## Find out which rule wins **What you are making:** a page with three lines of text in three different colours, where two CSS rules fight over the same paragraph and you get to see which one comes out on top. **Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are. 1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* > **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-specificity-yourname`. 1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**). 2. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-specificity-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-css-specificity-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project in VS Code In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** Down the left-hand side is a list of the files in this project: - `index.html` — your web page - `style.css` — how it looks - `script.js` — what it does For this assignment you edit **`index.html`** and **`style.css`**. --- ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** write two rules that both aim at the same paragraph, and watch which of them wins. This has two halves. Do them in order. **Half 1 — three lines of text (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Find the line that says `` and the line that says ``. Everything you add goes **between those two lines**. 3. Click at the end of a line between them and press **Enter** to make a new line. 4. Type these three lines, one under the other: ```html

This heading is never mentioned in the CSS.

This paragraph has no label.

This paragraph wears a label.

``` 5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. The last two lines are both paragraphs — the same `

` tag. The only difference is that the second one carries a label. That difference is the whole point of this task. **Half 2 — three rules that disagree (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this exactly: ```css body { color: grey; } p { color: blue; } .special { color: red; } ``` 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. **What each piece means:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `body { color: grey; }` | Sets the text colour for the whole page. Anything not told otherwise takes this colour from the body. That handing-down is called **inheritance**. | | `p { color: blue; }` | Aims at every paragraph by its tag name. This is the weakest kind of aim. | | `.special { color: red; }` | Aims at anything wearing the label `special`. The dot at the front is what makes it a label rather than a tag name. | | `color` | The colour of the lettering. `background-color` would be the colour behind it. | | `;` | Ends one instruction. Leave one out and the browser gives up on the rest of the rule. | The last paragraph is pulled at by two rules at once: `p` says blue, `.special` says red. They cannot both win. The **more particular** aim wins, and a label is more particular than a tag name, so that paragraph comes out **red**. The heading is a different story. No rule mentions `h2` at all, so it quietly takes the grey handed down from `body`. > You may use any three colour words, as long as they are three different ones so you can tell the rules apart. The label `special` must be spelled the same way in both files, with the dot only in the CSS. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. Three lines, three colours: the heading is grey, the first paragraph is blue, and the last paragraph is red. Now prove that the red one is not winning merely because it was typed last. 5. Go back to VS Code and click the `style.css` tab. Click once at the very start of the line `.special {`, hold the **Shift** key down, and click once at the end of the `}` two lines below it. Those three lines turn blue — that means they are selected. 6. Press **Ctrl + X** *(Mac: Command + X)*. The three lines vanish; they are being held for you. 7. Click on the empty line **above** the `p {` rule, then press **Ctrl + V** *(Mac: Command + V)*. The `.special` rule reappears, now **before** the `p` rule. 8. Save with **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. 9. The last paragraph is **still red**. Being more particular beat being written later. Either order passes the checker, so leave the rules wherever you prefer. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. No colour at all? Open `index.html` and look inside `` for a line reading ``. That line is what connects your two files — without it, the CSS is ignored. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Show a class beating an element" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | Both paragraphs are blue | The label is not on the second paragraph | It must read `

` — inside the opening tag, with no dot | | Both paragraphs are red | The label ended up on both paragraphs | Only the second `

` carries `class="special"` | | The last paragraph is blue rather than red | The dot is missing in the CSS | The rule must begin `.special {`, not `special {` | | The heading is black rather than grey | The colour was set on something other than `body` | The first rule must read `body { color: grey; }` | | Red cross on "has a class selector" | `style.css` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `style.css` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `index.html` has a `

` — no dot - [ ] `style.css` has a `body` rule that sets `color` - [ ] `style.css` has a `p` rule that sets `color` - [ ] `style.css` has a rule beginning `.special {` — with a dot - [ ] Every line inside a rule ends with `;` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs) - [ ] You can see three different colours in your browser
